speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) moved
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. C-123, to provide for the disposition of Indian claims.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the Minister would be happy to make a statement in this regard.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not agree that I am so happy about making a statement, but I did make certain commitments to the members of the committee who considered the resolution last night, and in fulfilment of these assurances, I think some remarks are appropriate at this time.
First I wish to thank the hon. Members who participated in the debate yesterday at the resolution stage of this bill. Needless to say I was encouraged by the unanimous expression of support of the resolution which came from all quarters of this House. That augurs well for the early passage and the success of this long overdue legislation.
As I said when I introduced the legislation yesterday, two joint committees of the two Houses of Parliament, one in the period 1946-48 and the other in the period 1959-61, after hearing the evidence of Indians and others concerned, strongly recommended that action be taken to deal with this problem.
It was decided both by the former administration and by this administration that steps should be taken to implement the recommendations of those two joint committees to establish an Indian Claims Commission. As was mentioned more than once yesterday, legislation was drafted and introduced in this House in December, 1963. Following this the proposed legislation was sent to Indian organizations, band councils and other interested groups across Canada for study and for suggestions as to improvements to these provisions. This was done during the year 1964 and during the first month or two of this year. Some 300 briefs and letters concerning the proposed legislation were received. These were reviewed and, as hon. Members, who have had an opportunity to peruse this bill and compare it with the older one will see, certain major changes have been made which I think will commend themselves to all Members of this House.
DEBATES	2749
Indian Claims Commission
I should like to refer briefly to the main provisions of this new Bill C-123. First of all, the Commission will comprise five members, the chairman to be trained in the law, with experience on the bench or at the bar. There was a suggestion made that the chairman should be an international jurist selected by the United Nations. In fact the hon. Member for Skeena put forward that suggestion again last night. However, while those of us who have considered the representations feel strongly that the Chairman should be a person with adequate training and experience, we do believe there are persons in Canada who are eminently qualified to perform the duties of chairman of an Indian Claims Commission that is functioning solely in this country.
There were other suggestions made as to the qualifications of the Commissioners. Some thought that such persons should be trained in anthropology, ethnology and sociology-I remember hearing mention of a lot of other "ologies" during that discussion-and history and economics. There were many representations to the effect that an Indian should be appointed to the Commission and, as you will see from a perusal of the bill, we have accepted that suggestion. Provision has been made for one of the Commissioners to be appointed from among persons who are defined as Indians under the Indian Act. e (3:20 p.m.)
However, it is not considered desirable to specify in the legislation the discipline in which any Commissioner other than the chairman must have been trained. But we are going to have a chairman trained in the law. We are also going to have at least one Indian on this commission of five. In the new bill we have made provision for a vice chairman, who may exercise all the powers and functions of the chairman if he is absent or unable to act for any reason. I think this is also an improvement which came out of suggestions that have been made.
Each Commissioner may be appointed-not "shall be"-but may be for a term not exceeding 10 years. We do not say "shall be" because if you were going to appoint a man in his late sixties or early seventies you might not want to appoint him for such a period as would mean he would serve beyond the age of 75, which is the limit for all judges in the superior courts of this country. However, he can be appointed for a term of 10 years.
June 22. 1965

Indian Claims Commission It was suggested in some briefs that this Commission should be made permanent, and that no time limit should be put on its life. But we must keep in mind, Mr. Speaker, that the purpose of this Commission is to deal with claims which have arisen in the past, not new claims but claims that have arisen in the past. And while no Commissioner may be appointed for a term exceeding 10 years, if the Commission has not completed its work and if a member has served the full term of 10 years there is no reason why he should not be appointed for another term not exceeding two years, if he is doing a good job. This provision will permit the reappointment of one or more Commissioners when their terms expire. But I can assure this House that the Commission itself will go on until the last claim has been determined, and not until then will the Commission cease to function.
I hope this will not take 10 years, but based on the experience of our neighbouring republic to the south it may well take longer because, as I have learned in the last four months, some of the claims are very complicated. They will take months or longer in preparation, and it will take some time for the Commission to deal with the very complicated and involved claims that have come in from different parts of the country.
A word or two might be in order about the classes of claims. The classes of claims that may be brought are very broad, sufficiently broad, it seems to me, that known claims arising out of any past events can be heard. In 1948 the joint committee recommended that the Commission deal with claims under treaties. The 1961 joint committee recommended that the British Columbia land question and the Oka land dispute be heard by the Commission. Under the bill as drafted the kinds of claims that both joint committees had in mind have been included, and we have gone even further than that.
There are now five general classes of claims, which may be brought. First there are claims that land was taken without Indian aboriginal interest having been extinguished. This is the kind of claim that has been advanced by the Indians of my Province of British Columbia and which is commonly known as the B.C. land question. This was referred to at some length in the report of the 1961 committee on Indian Affairs.
The second class of claims covers claims that lands set apart as reserves for Indians were disposed of without compensation, or 
compensation so inadequate as to be unconscionable. We heard several references to that type of claim in the debate last night on the resolution. There have been many allegations that reserve lands have been improperly disposed of without compensation being paid, or that the compensation was inequitable. Suggestions were made, which I might say appealed to me at first when I was making a study of the matter, that the use of the word "unconscionable" would make it difficult to prove a claim based on the inadequacy of compensation, because as long as there was some substantial or almost reasonable compensation it might be argued that it was not unconscionable.
I might say that point troubled me at first but when I went into the history of the matter I found that similar language is used in the United States legislation, and that there have been a number of successful claims in the United States involving inadequacy of compensation as the basis of an allegation of unconscionable conduct. It is reasonable to assume that such an interpretation will be placed upon the word by the Commission or other bodies dealing with the matter in this country.
The third class covers claims that the Crown failed to discharge any obligation to Indians arising under any treaty, agreement or undertaking. Last night several hon. Members, including the hon. Member for Peace River and I think the hon. Member for Comox-Alberni, referred to this point. Provision is made in the new bill to consider allegations that the Crown has failed to live up to its obligations to Indians under any treaty, agreement or undertaking. This provision will enable bands that believe treaties have been abrogated in any way to make a claim; or if they feel that any other agreement or undertaking with them has not been fully discharged they may also bring a claim. May we have order, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Order please.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The fourth class consists of claims that moneys held by the Crown in trust for Indians were improperly used. Some have alleged maladministration of trust funds. Where a band feels that such is the case it may bring a claim. These four classes cover claims involving aboriginal land rights, reserve lands, band funds and treaty obligations. Finally, in order to ensure as far as possible that any other matter which does not fall in the above four categories can be heard, there is a further provision for claims
June 22, 1965	COMMONS
based on the alleged failure of the Crown to act fairly and honourably with Indians in some transactions, thereby causing injury to them.
It will be seen that the classes of claims that may be brought under this bill are very broad and will permit the hearing of claims of alleged wrongs against Indians in the collective sense. The collective interest of the Indian is represented by the Indian band, and this is set out clearly in the bill. Claims of individual Indians are not included, although there have been suggestions that they should be. However, if there is any individual alive today who feels he has such a claim he can seek his remedy in the courts. The same is not true of Indians in their collective capacity with respect to claims arising out of treaties made 150 years ago, 100 years ago, 75 years ago or possibly even 25 years ago. Therefore under the bill such claims must be put forward by Indian bands. There is probably no individual Indian living today who is directly affected, so I think the question of the individual becomes academic. However, by making it possible for an Indian band as an identifiable group to seek redress, their rights as a group are recognized.
There were also suggestions that claims might be permitted against the Crown in right of a province. For constitutional and jurisdictional reasons obviously this has not been included. However, claims arising during the preconfederation period may be heard as well as all claims against Canada since Confederation.
I might say a word or two about claimants with particular reference to clause 6 of the bill.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
As I have said, claims may be brought on behalf of Indian bands. Normally the band council, as the duly constituted authority to act on behalf of the band, will put forward the claim. In some cases, however, there are no councils, and accordingly the chief will be in a position to bring the claim on behalf of the band. There may be a few cases where there is no band council nor a chief, and in in such cases any adult member of the band may bring the claim, provided the Commission is satisfied he has been authorized by the band to do so. Provision is also made for bringing claims in cases where the bands, in the past, have either been amalgamated with other bands or have been divided to form two or more bands. These bands, through their
DEBATES	2751
Indian Claims Commission authorized responsible councils or their authorized spokesmen, will be able to bring claims.
I might say there were suggestions in some of the briefs and letters that were submitted, as well as in a telegram I received today, that Indian organizations should be able to bring claims on behalf of the Indians of a province. This was also mentioned last night. I may say this suggestion was given very careful consideration, and the conclusion reached was that this would pose insurmountable difficulties because Indian organizations, being purely voluntary organizations, do not necessarily represent a particular band or group of Indians. For instance, you will find in my native Province of New Brunswick, Indians of several different tribes. The same situation applies in Nova Scotia, as well as in practically every province of Canada. Where you have a band having a specific claim with regard to the disposition of some land that has been reserved for its use, you may well have another group with entirely conflicting views. This suggestion, therefore, after most careful consideration has been rejected, or at least has not been incorporated in the Bill now up for second reading.
The membership of Indian organizations, I might say, in the short time I have been Minister-and I have met several of them- fluctuates from day to day, from month to month and certainly from year to year. Conflicts of interest could arise where one or more organizations decided on their own initiative that they were the true representatives of a particular group or band of Indians. On the other hand, the band is well defined. In most cases the Indian bands had lands set apart for their use. They have a well defined membership, a membership that is established and maintained by law.
I might say that while for the reasons I have given we have not seen fit to include Indian organizations in the Bill, or make it possible for them to be claimants, this does not mean that Indian organizations might not take the initiative and advise the band or the chief to bring a claim. They could assist the band council or the chief or the adult, if the Claims Commission directed that an adult could represent a band, in the filing and prosecution of a claim. It may well be, and I think probably will be, that this will be the role that many Indian organizations may wish to play. There is nothing in the provisions of the Bill that prevents them from doing so. They can do all these things, but they cannot be claimants. On the other hand, I reiterate
June 22, 1965

Indian Claims Commission that we certainly do not feel Indian organizations, with their fluctuating membership, should be permitted to present claims to the Commission.
There is another important matter to which attention was drawn in the briefs that were submitted, Mr. Speaker. I refer to the time limit for filing claims. There has been considerable publicity given to the establishment of an Indian Claims Commission during the last few years. For several years it has been the announced policy of successive governments to establish a Commission. The purpose of the Commission, as I stated yesterday and I believe I reiterated today, is to clear grievances from the past. On the whole I believe the great majority of Indians know what their grievances are. They have talked about them enough over all my adult life. Accordingly, in order to bring some finality to this matter that has been in the air for at least 40 or 50 years, we believe that claims should be filed within a reasonable period of time. The previous Bill, No. C-130, provided that claims must be filed within two years after the act comes into force.
There were many suggestions regarding this limitation, ranging from suggestions of two years to no time limit at all. Some people were recommending a permanent Commission. Some arguments were advanced that the time limit for filing claims was too short, particularly since some bands seemed to think they not only must file their claims within the time limit but they must also prepare all the documentation necessary to support the claim. This is not the case. Only a notice of the claim need be filed, setting out what the claim is about with reasonable certainty. The documentation can follow later.
However, to meet the basic objection that the time limit of two years originally contemplated was too short, the time limit established in subclause 2 of clause 6 of the bill has now been extended to three years. It is considered this is a reasonable time within which to file a notice of claim. It may not be heard for five years, but they must give notice within three years. In the light of all the publicity that has been given to the Indian Claims bill, more particularly by the distribution of Bill No. C-130 in 1964 and the publicity we propose to give the establishment of the Commission when the bill becomes law, I would hope Members would agree that three years is a generous time.
One of the most far reaching and most novel provisions in the bill is the one having to do

with the nature of the evidence that may be considered by the Commission. An important principle embodied in the bill is the fact that the Commission will not be bound by the ordinary rules of evidence. This is most important, since the Commission in its work will be able to dispense with the rules of evidence which in the past resulted in the rejection of some evidence relating to claims. Having practised law for more than two decades before I went into business I realize that in cases such as we have here, where most of the claims arose in the last century or perhaps even earlier, if we adhered to the strict rules of evidence there would be no possibility for these claimants to get justice. Some of the evidence that may be submitted may not be accepted in ordinary courts of law, yet it may be credible and trustworthy. It was considered necessary, in view of the antiquity of some of the claims, that such evidence be allowed.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Perhaps I might pause to interject that we have all had our own experience of somebody telling us an incident. Our parents may tell us of an incident; when we pass it on to somebody else there is usually a slight variation, and when it is passed on to our children and our grandchildren there will be even more variations. So, while people may repeat in good faith claims and stories they have heard, in some instances these might be so far removed from the truth that they are almost fairy stories.
I am not suggesting that would happen here, but it is important that where oral evidence does not exist, because there is no person alive today who could give the testimony, there must be some evidence to support the claim, something contemporaneous with the origin of the claim. It was thought that it would be unwise if the claim were supported by oral evidence only. It should be corroborated in some material way by other than oral evidence, that is by something to show that the oral evidence was true or was likely to be true. This could be an artifact, a marking, or some other corroborative evidence. The question of what weight should be given to testimony is being left to the Commission to decide.
With respect to the production of papers, I hardly think it is necessary to deal with this question at any length. The Commission will be authorized to make rules respecting its procedures and will be given such powers, rights and privileges as are vested in a
June 22, 1965	COMMONS
superior court of record in respect of the difficult question of the production and inspection of documents, procedures for the bringing of claims and powers as to attendance, summoning and the examination of witnesses.
In some of the briefs, it was suggested that direction be given to the Commission as to the kind of evidence it would entertain and the weight to be attached to such evidence. There were also suggestions that there be detailed provisions with respect to the production of documents. It was considered, however, after full examination that it should be left to the Commission to determine what, in the light of practice, would be necessary to provide the claimants with full and reasonable opportunity to prepare their claims and be heard; and that the Commission should also determine what testimony it would hear and what weight it would give to such testimony.
Because of the nature of the claims, and because the problems that might be encountered in dealing with them cannot be foreseen, it is considered that it would be impractical to try to prescribe in a detailed way what the Commission shall do with respect to evidence, documents and the examination of witnesses. It is expected that the Commission will hold hearings in various parts of the country and, as required, may conduct special investigations into any particular aspects of a claim.
Another significant innovation and great improvement in this bill as compared with the former one is the provision for assistance to Indian bands in bringing claims. Provision is made in the bill for providing assistance to Indian bands that do not have sufficient available resources to enable them to bring a claim before the Commission or to pursue or oppose an appeal. There would be no point in setting up a commission if destitute bands could not get the lawyers, anthropologists and other research experts that they may need.
It so happens that there are a few Indian bands which are very wealthy, either through possessing land which made choice sites for industrial purposes or through the discovery of oil and gas. Such bands will also have claims to put forward and will be in a position to do so, but other adjoining bands in a province could not make claims unless assistance were provided them.
One of the fundamental problems that we had to consider was whether Indian bands would be able to finance the cost of having their claims adequately investigated, documented and presented before the Commission.
DEBATES	2753
Indian Claims Commission In many cases this will involve not only legal advisers and counsel but research personnel as well. The real problem is how to assist those bands that may not be able to finance in whole or in part the bringing of their claims.
Having determined that bands unable to finance their own claims should be assisted, the question arose as to how such assistance might best be made available. I may say it did not take long for the officials who were advising me or for me to decide that the administration of such assistance could not be associated with the Department of Indian Affairs, even though I may have a very high opinion of my own integrity; nor should it be associated with the Department of Justice, which will have the responsibility of defending the Crown. It was therefore considered that the most appropriate way in which the assistance might be provided would be to make it the responsibility of the Indian Claims Commission, and to assure the Commission that it would have funds to do this work.
Mr. Speaker, may we have order?

The Commission will set the terms and conditions of the assistance to be provided, whether in the form of direct assistance, such as by way of research staff, or financial assistance to help pay for research and legal counsel. Provision is made so that a band desiring help will be able to make application for assistance to prepare and bring a claim before the Commission, or for assistance in any of the appeal proceedings or further hearings that may be held as provided in the bill. In special circumstances, the Commission is given power to forgive all or part of the financial assistance so provided. The scheme of assistance as set out in the bill will, I believe, go a long way toward meeting the expressed requests of many band councils and others.
It is not possible to determine in advance how much might need to be provided to meet all the requests for financial assistance that might be made. June 22, 1965

Indian Claims Commission cover any requests for assistance that might be made to the Commission during the current fiscal year.
The Commission will be required to render a decision on each claim, setting forth its reasons therefor and awarding money compensation where it is warranted. The Commission can make a money award only. There were suggestions that it be given the power to restore land, or to award both land and money, and also to make declaratory orders in respect of treaty obligations.
It was not intended that the Claims Commission would take the place of ordinary courts in determining points of law such as the validity and effect of an Indian treaty. [DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
The Commission is now being given wide powers, however, to determine whether an obligation under a treaty as determined by the courts has been discharged. The restoration of land may be quite impossible for any number of reasons. Land may have been patented years ago. I know that a project in southwestern Ontario with which I was associated for some years, and which is now the hub of a billion dollar industry, is all established on a former Indian reserve. Even if there has been some flaw in a title of this kind, it will be impossible to return land where patents have been issued. But if there has been an injustice the Commission will be able to give the band or bands concerned adequate compensation. There is no limit to the amount of compensation which can be awarded.
As regards the suggestion that declaratory orders may be made in respect to treaty applications, it is considered that such orders can quite properly be dealt with in the ordinary courts in accordance with the established rules of legal evidence. It would be a case of interpreting a document.
A word as to appeals. The Commission will sit and decide on the merits of these claims. The decisions of the Commission are final and conclusive, subject to appeal to a special Indian Claims Appeal Court which is being constituted under this bill. The Commission being a tribunal which is not bound by legal rules of evidence, and not applying facts to existing law or being guided by established principles, there are no grounds on which an appeal could be taken to the Supreme Court or to the Exchequer Court. It could not possibly be done. But all judges of the Exchequer Court are to be ex officio judges of the Indian Claims Appeal Court and are to be given authority to confirm or vary decisions of the 
Commission, or they may refer claims back to the Commission for further hearing.
Apart from the appeal to the Indian Claims Appeal Court as to the reasonableness of an award, provision is made for reference to the Exchequer Court on questions of jurisdiction, and for appeals from the Exchequer Court to the Supreme Court in respect of any such decision concerning a question of jurisdiction.
A word on the subject of awards. This is dealt with in clauses 9, 10 and 11. Where the Commission finds that the claim of an Indian band is justified in whole or in part, it may make a money award. In determining the amount of the award the Commission shall take into account the amount of any moneys already paid or the money value of any other compensation given to the band in respect of the matter out of which the claim arose. This is where the question of unconscionable transactions arises. For example, if the Commission were to find that band X was entitled to Y dollars under the provisions of some treaty or agreement but had in fact received only Z dollars, then it would take into account the amount Z already paid when determining the amount of the award.
I turn now to the disposition of funds. Any amount which may be awarded by the Commission or fixed by the Indian Claims Appeal Court will be paid into the capital fund of the Indian band concerned to be used for the purposes to which the capital funds of a band may be devoted. The purposes for which expenditures of capital funds may be made are prescribed under the Indian Act. In general, the funds may be used only for purposes of benefit to all members of the band; a percentage can be used for per capita distribution, but the total amount cannot be dissipated in this way. Of course before payment of an award can be made to a band fund, money must be appropriated by Parliament for that purpose. Once the moneys have been paid over the claim will be deemed to have been discharged. The reasons for placing restrictions on the use of band funds is obvious. The fund is the property of the band as a whole, and not only the present generation but their children and grandchildren have to be considered.
In summary, may I say it is felt that the tribunal which is being established will enable a final determination to be made as to the claims of all Indian bands. We must realize that this Commission has a monumental task ahead of it. And when the last
June 22, 1965

claim has been settled we hope old controversies will be laid at rest, and this should go a long way toward rebuilding the kind of confidence in the intentions of Parliament and of the people of Canada which is absolutely necessary if we are to do our work for the future development and welfare of the Indian people.
I hope that this legislation which is so vital to the settlement of Indian claims will help achieve this end.
As I assured the Committee yesterday, as soon as this bill has been given second reading I intend to ask that it be referred to a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons for examination and report, and I am prepared to move the appropriate resolution at the earliest opportunity.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I think I should commend the Minister for the careful and detailed statement he has given to us on the motion for second reading of this bill in connection with a contentious, difficult and tenacious problem which has existed over a great many years. The measure deals with a problem to which I do not think there will ever be a complete and equitable solution, though by the terms of this legislation the Government intends to move as far as it possibly can in that direction.
I think, too, I must commend the officials of the Minister who undoubtedly participated to a large extent in the preparation of this legislation following the numerous briefs and representations which I am sure were made to them and which, I am convinced, must have raised a great many difficulties.
My own disposition is to give guarded and somewhat reserved approval to this motion, subject to what I shall have to say later in the expectation that a measure of this kind is one which must bristle with legal questions based on varying interpretations of the different clauses to which the hon. gentleman has referred. Some of these will no doubt be passed on the Claims Commission itself. It seems to me that only by means of a joint committee such as has been suggested will it be possible to give this legislation the careful and detailed study which its great importance deserves.
I hope when the Minister closes the debate he will refer to the proposal I made yesterday, that the Government should indicate its good faith in this issue by expressing willingness to comply with the recommendations which may be made by the joint committee concerning changes and alterations. I have this in mind

Indian Claims Commission when I indicate my own view that the bill is one to which in principle we may give our qualified acceptance.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Having said that, to indicate the nature of the reservations I have I should like to refer to several of the matters which I think are of very considerable importance and which will require clarification and a more detailed statement by those who will be appearing before the committee during the course of the study of this bill. I am not blaming the Minister for this, but the bill came into my hands only about half an hour or so before the opening of the House. It is a very lengthy bill comprising 32 clauses involving in many cases new departures, and for this reason I feel I must qualify my acceptance of it.
Some of the things I wish to refer to, which I assume will be the subject of study and consideration by the committee, are these. First of all, may I bring to the attention of the Minister that in the interpretation clause "band" means a body of Indians that is a band for the purposes of the Indian Act. I point out that while it is apparent from this interpretation that there is a limitation in this legislation to Indians within the Indian Act, this leaves a very considerable omission in that the bill fails to take into consideration the Eskimos of northern Quebec and the Northwest Territories, in respect of whom there have been no treaties signed and who are now in the position of having in many cases to give up their birthrights in respect of the material assets and real property in the areas in which they reside without any agreement being reached at all. This, of course, is not a matter within the Minister's jurisdiction, but as Minister charged with responsibility under the Indian Act I think this very signal omission should be called to the attention of the Government.
I have no comment to make at this time with respect to the suggestions advanced as to the personnel of the Commission. I think there has been an improvement in this respect, in that there is now to be at least one Indian, within the meaning of the Indian Act, among the commissioners. The qualifications which the Minister mentioned are a condition precedent. I think they have been well put, and I have no inclination to quarrel with him on this score.
When we reach the duties of the Commission as set out in clause 5 of the bill we come to the very heart of the problem. I would
June 22. 1965

Indian Claims Commission be of the opinion that certain clarification might be required in connection with some of the areas which are the subject of the proposed jurisdiction of the Claims Commission. Subclause (a) of clause 5 refers to claims which may be brought in respect of-
-lands in any area that now forms part of Canada-
-which were taken from Indians by the Crown, and so on, without any agreement or undertaking to give compensation. It seems to me at first blush that the word "adequate" should be inserted before the word "compensation"; because any compensation at all, no matter how inadequate, would disqualify an application being made under subclause (a). Subclause (b) says that claims may be advanced in respect of-
-lands set apart for the use and benefit of Indians in any area-
-I assume that refers to lands set apart as reserves and which subsequently were granted, sold or otherwise disposed of by the Crown. I also assume it includes the natural resources and the mineral rights under the land as well, and I think this is a matter subject to litigation at the present time in the Province of Alberta. The subclause continues:
-and no compensation was given in respect thereof to such Indians or the compensation given was so inadequate as to he unconscionable;
In other words a very heavy onus is thus laid upon the Indians and the band to establish, before any right is vested in the Claims Commission to make an award, that the compensation given was so inadequate as to be unconscionable. I think this is rather anomalous, because it is essential for the band to prove this in order to get into court, if I may use that expression, or, to get before the Claims Commission. But once they have the right to come to the Claims Commission, I would judge that the Commission may make an award which may be reasonable and adequate in their opinion. I think the provision, that they have to establish to the satisfaction of the Claims Commission that the compensation given was so inadequate as to be unconscionable lays a very heavy onus on a band. One must suggest that this is an area where there might be some discussion during the course of the committee's deliberations.
I am very pleased to see subclause (d) of clause 5 in the bill. We had an interesting discussion on this matter yesterday. The hon. Member for Northwest Territories and other hon. Members who spoke brought this subject to the attention of the Minister. The inten-

tion is that this subject shall be covered by subclause (d) in any situation where there has been a breach of a treaty; and this despite the fact that by what now appears to be a decision of the highest court of this land there is no legal restriction against a Government legislating, if it sees fit, in any way so as to vary the terms of a treaty, or to legislate in such a way that there is no longer any compliance with the terms of a treaty.
This brings up another problem which I think is serious, and where I now feel there might not be that complete compliance which I would hope would be present. Subclause (d) is to the effect that a claim may be advanced where the Crown failed to discharge any obligations arising under any treaty to Indians living in an area that forms part of Canada. The meaning of the word "obligation" is involved here. If this is construed to mean, as it well could, a legal obligation, then subclause (d) has no value at all. I feel that for a 100 per cent opportunity to be given to Indians and Indian bands to seek and obtain a remedy for breach of a treaty the word "obligation" should be followed by "or promise". I throw out that suggestion to the Minister for his consideration. I do not want to be splitting hairs, but I want to make it quite plain that I am sure from time to time there would be constructions sought of the various parts of this legislation, and to me the words "obligation" connotes a legal obligation.
The question arises, because of the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada to which I referred, whether there is any longer, if there was ever at any time, any legal obligation on Canada to fulfil the terms of these treaties. An obligation in honour, in equity, in decency, yes; but there is a question in my mind as to whether there is now a real obligation within the meaning of the word as it appears in subclause (d).
With regard to the length of time within which a claim may be brought, I understand there might be a conflict of views on this. I would be prepared to accept three years provided the Minister might consider adding the words "or such further time as the Commission might recommend". It seems to me there may be very special and unusual circumstances where a band may be unable to gather together the evidence, or where there may be some conflict. I can think of a number of reasons whereby the band might fail to bring proceedings within the term of three years. It would not be unreasonable to grant the Commission the right to extend the time
June 22, 1965

if a proper case was made to it. This is something the Minister might well consider, because it would really not do much violence to the meaning at this time, but it would provide an extra safeguard.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
In legislation of this kind there must be the most liberal and generous construction possible. I commend the position that has been taken, that the usual rigid legal rules of evidence shall not apply. However, this position is subject, of course, to subclause 1 in respect of which, as the Minister pointed out, no award shall be made unless there is evidence in writing that is reasonably contemporaneous to the time the subject matter of the claim arose. I understand the reasoning behind this, which relates to the general principle that no one shall be entitled to manufacture evidence in writing to support his own claim, but evidence in writing which was made at a time fairly close to the time when the claim arose could not be considered as being manufactured in respect of proceedings which will not take place until many years later. I think the whole thing depends on an interpretation of the word "reasonably". Certainly there must be some distinction made, but I hope in its decisions the Commission will not construe this word "reasonably" too rigidly against the Indians making the claims.
In clause 13 there is provision for an appeal to the Exchequer Court on the grounds of jurisdiction. This is a very reasonable provision and provides a simple and expeditious method whereby either the Crown or the banks may seek the opinion of the Exchequer Court as to whether any claim made comes within the provisions of clause 5. The appeal from the Exchequer Court to the Supreme Court is also quite reasonable.
Under subclause 2 of clause 14 I suggest there should be the inclusion of the same saving provision I referred to earlier. This subclause states:
No appeal lies after leave therefor has been obtained under subsection (1) unless it is entered in the Supreme Court within sixty days from the making of the order granting leave to appeal.
Having in mind that many of the Indian bands live in areas which are very considerable distances from the places where these courts are held, I think it would be wise to add after the word "appeal" some saving words to the effect that this time can be extended if in the opinion of the Supreme Court of Canada a case has been made to do so. I

Indian Claims Commission should not like to see this 60-day period left in its present terms.
The Indian Claims Appeal Court I think is an innovation. It is very desirable and gives an opportunity both for the Crown and the bands to appeal on the ground that an award was unreasonable.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, in respect of the question of costs, I think the Minister made it reasonably clear that provided the Commission is satisfied, on application by a band, that it simply does not have these resources, all that is required in forming and preparing its case-engaging counsel, calling witnesses and bringing witnesses to the place of the trial; in other words, everything which in any sense of the word is a condition precedent to the band being able to make an adequate, fair and full presentation of its case- will be made available, in terms of the money required, to the Indian band or bands making the application for an award. Anything less than that would certainly be unreasonable, unfair and restrictive in respect of benefits which might flow from this legislation.
Before I leave this subject there is one other point in clause 32 which deals with the question of assistance to Indians. While there is nothing specifically stated, I would assume, and perhaps the Minister can clarify this, that in the event the Indians making application are unsuccessful, there will be no question that costs will be awarded against them. That is an inference we can possibly take from clause 32, but I am sure the Minister is willing to make this point clear beyond any shadow of doubt; that in the event an application is unsuccessful, no costs under any circumstances can be assessed against the applicant band.
The remarks I have made represent a general indication of some of the problems involved, and I have not touched on them all, which can only be adequately and properly disposed of when the matter is before a joint committee to which officials of the Department are made available for questioning. I assume it will be possible for that committee to have access to the officials of the Department of Justice in order to consider some of the legal problems which could arise in connection with the interpretation and construction of this legislation. We must do this with the understanding that no stone will be left unturned to assure that the blot on our nation, in respect of the claims of Indians which can be brought within the four corners of this legis-
June 22, 1965

Indian Claims Commission lation, is, as far as it possibly can be, erased forever.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not that anxious to vote for the bill or to let it pass without comment.

In the Minister's opening remarks on second reading he indicated that he welcomed what he termed the unanimous support for the bill that was given yesterday at the resolution stage. If the Minister made that comment sincerely I do not think he could have been listening to what was said, because there was not unanimous support for the bill. There was not unanimous support because we had not seen it and did not know just what it would contain and whether it would be worth while supporting. If the Minister will read the comments of the hon. Member for Comox-Alberni, who spoke first for the New Democratic Party, he will see there was no endorsation of the bill, nor did I indicate that we would support the bill. There was no unanimous endorsation of the bill, but rather an expression of the fact that this was perhaps the most important piece of legislation with which we would be dealing at this session.
In my view, yesterday and today are but further sad and sorry days for the native Indian people. When the contents of the bill became public for the first time last night the hopes of a great number of Indian people in Canada that finally they were going to get a fair hearing and justice and equity at the hands of Government were dashed to the ground. I would not be saying this if this were the first time a bill to set up an Indian claims commission had been presented to the House. It is not the first time. As is well known, Bill No. C-130 was presented in December of 1963. That bill was roundly condemned as inadequate by large numbers of Indian people, and with few exceptions the bill now before us is identical with Bill No. C-130 introduced in 1963.
In the intervening period the Indian people, whose views had been sought and whose ideas and proposed amendments had been solicited, had hopes that their proposals and suggestions for amendments to Bill C-130 would be accepted with the result that the new bill would be drafted in such a way as to establish a commission which would be able to deal properly, fairly and adequately with their longstanding grievances. They discovered last night that this was not the case. They discovered last night that the bill before us is just the same as Bill C-130 so far as is substance is concerned and the establishment of a commission which, properly and fairly, will be able to hear and adjudicate upon the claims of the native Indian people.
June 22, 1965

Last night we issued a press statement about the bill under the names of the leader of the New Democratic Party, myself, the hon. Member for Comox-Alberni, the hon. Member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands and the hon. Member for Winnipeg North. I should like to quote one or two paragraphs from that press statement because I think it succinctly sums up our position with respect to the bill and the Government that has introduced it:
The provisions of the bill introduced tonight by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration which provides for the establishment of an Indian Claims Commission make it obvious that the Government has been speaking with a forked tongue and that it is firmly entrenched in the position of a modem day combination "land-grabber and whiskey-peddler".
There is no change of substance in Bill C-123 over Bill C-130, which was introduced on December 14, 1963, that would permit the Commission to be fair and equitable in hearing and deciding upon claims presented to it. There are, however, two important changes. One is that an Indian shall be a member of the Commission and the other is that financial assistance shall be given to bands to prepare and present their claims.
It seems obvious that the Government in Bill C-130 of 1963 deliberately refused to accept these two suggestions in order that it could spend a year and a half listening to submissions by Indian people, then offer them something as a sop. Even some of the early day rum runners were more subtle than this.
The press release goes on to deal in some detail with the bill itself and in fact is an identical reproduction of a similar statement which was made with respect to Bill C-130. The statement can be similar because the bills are identical with the exception of the two points I mentioned and one or two other extremely minor technical changes.
The history of the dealing of governments with the Indian people includes, of course, their dealings with the Indian people of British Columbia, those with whom I am most familiar and who I believe by and large have the greatest single complaint to make about treatment at the hands of Government in that because there were no treaties with the Indians in British Columbia, they are now faced and have been continuously faced with what is commonly called the B.C. Indian land question. There was no war against the Indian people of British Columbia by which territory was won. There were no treaties, no negotiations, nothing except simple encroachment upon lands exploited and owned, in the sense that the Indians understand that word, by the Indian people of British Columbia.
In 1910 Sir Wilfrid Laurier promised the Indian people of British Columbia that the

Indian Claims Commission Indian land question would be taken to the Privy Council. Sir Wilfrid Laurier did not do that. In the eyes of the Indian people who were affected Sir Wilfrid Laurier told them a lie. In their eyes the Liberal party of that day was deceitful, and it looks like they are not improving with the passage of time.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
In 1913 a group of native Indian people from the Nishga tribe, or what is now the Nishga tribal council, prepared a petition for the presentation of their claim to the Privy Council. Eventually the Federal Government got around to attempting to deal with their petition, and in 1914 they passed an order in council with relation to the matter. The contents of this order in council are important because they indicate what the attitude of the Government of that day was with respect to the legitimate claims of the Indian people. By order in council P.C. 751 of June 20, 1914, the Governor in Council resolved to refer the Indian land claims to the Exchequer Court of Canada. We have not progressed too much, since we are now likely to end up in the hands of the Exchequer Court of Canada.
One of the provisions of the order in council is as follows:
The Indians of British Columbia shall, by their chiefs or representatives, in a binding way, agree, if the court or on appeal the Privy Council, decides that they have a title to the lands of the Province, to surrender such title, receiving from the Dominion benefits to be granted for extinguishment of title in accordance with past usage of the Crown in satisfying Indian claims in the unsurrendered territories-
In other words, what they meant was that the Dominion Government in 1914 wanted the Indian people to say before they went to court that if they won they would agree to lose; that if they won their case they would agree to accept the provisions contained in the treaties to which the hon. Member for Peace River referred yesterday, and to which the hon. Member for the Northwest Territories also made reference. In other words, in 1914 the Dominion Government was quite prepared to continue extinguishing the Indians' title to lands in the same niggardly dishonourable way that had been the case prior to that time. Naturally the Indian people rejected this suggestion, because it was unfair and because it was not in any sense of the word justice to them.
Subsequent to that we had the McKenna Royal Commission established between the provincial and federal governments without consultation with the Indian people, without their agreement and, at least on the surface,
June 22, 1965

Indian Claims Commission apparently without any concern for representations from the Indian people. The McKenna Royal Commission sat for some three or four years and went all over British Columbia. They made a report which subsequently found its way into the statute books of Canada and of the Province of British Columbia. These statutes, by their very existence, allegedly settled the British Columbia Indian land question. The Parliament of Canada and the legislature of British Columbia passed laws which in effect extinguished the claim of the Indian people of British Columbia to that land. They did not extinguish anything, because the claim is still there and now we have the Government of the day admitting the claim is still there and indicating its desire to give the people an opportunity to present their claims. This was another way for the Government to deal deceitfully and dishonourably with the legitimate claim of the native people of British Columbia.
In 1926 a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons was appointed to inquire into the claims of the allied Indian tribes of British Columbia who had petitioned Parliament in June, 1926 for redress, for justice and fair play. I have read the report of that joint Senate and House of Commons Committee. I have read the questions asked by the members of that Committee, and it is obvious from reading the verbatim report of those proceedings that the members of the committee had made up their collective minds before they even heard the case. They had decided before they heard the claim presented that there was not going to be an acceptance of any claim. They did not recommend that there was no claim, but they stated that the Indians had failed to prove their case.
However, they said, "Even though you have failed to prove your case we will recommend a cash settlement of $100,000 a year in lieu of treaty money." They said in effect, "You have no claim but we recognize you have a claim and we will give you $100,000 per year". This was the origin of the so-called British Columbia special vote in lieu of treaty.
Even though that joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons determined that the Indian people had not proved their claim, they still did not extinguish in the minds of the Indian people the thought that they had a just claim. They presented these ideas to the joint committee in 1946, 1947

and 1948, I believe it was. In 1948, as the Minister stated, that committee reported unanimously that there should be an Indian Claims Commission established. It is interesting to note that there was a Liberal Government in office at that time, and they failed to pay attention to the recommendation of the committee in 1948.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in so far as the British Columbia Indian land question is concerned, the native people of British Columbia do not need an Indian Claims Commission. They do not need an appeal court. They do not need this structure which is now before us. Canada does not need it. All that is required is a simple and honest declaration on the part of the Government that the hereditary or aboriginal title of the native people of British Columbia was never extinguished. This is all that is necessary, the admission of an historical fact. This could be followed by a discussion on a gentleman to gentleman basis, negotiation if you wish, to extinguish the claim of the native people of British Columbia. This is all that is required, a simple, honest acceptance of an historical fact. If the Minister believes implicitly in what he said a few moments ago about fair play and justice, this is precisely what he and his Government will do.
We do not need to put the native people to the trouble, expense, worry and time of preparing and arguing a case before the Commission when the cards are stacked against them by the very construction of the Commission. We do not need to put them to that difficulty. All that is required is the admission of the historical fact that the aboriginal title has never been extinguished, and then follow that up by some gentlemanly negotiations to conclude the matter. This is all that is required so far as the people of British Columbia are concerned.
The Liberal Party prepared a platform in 1962-63 with regard to this Indian Claims Commission. Reference has been made to it before in this chamber, and I should like to take one or two extracts from the pamphlet covering that platform to indicate that there is a vast difference between what the Government is saying now and what was set out in this pamphlet. I quote:
At Prince Rupert in 1910, Sir Wilfrid promised that the Indian land question would be taken to the Privy Council.
It never got there. It has puzzled me to understand why the Liberal Party would admit such a thing about Sir Wilfrid, that he
June 22, 1965	COMMONS
was dishonest in his dealings with the native people. I quote:
With the objective of achieving a fair and just settlement of all outstanding claims, it is Liberal policy that the Commission will include qualified authorities on British constitutional law as it affects aboriginal, hereditary and usufructory rights.
I should like to hear some declaration from the Minister concerning the personnel of this Commission in order to ascertain whether it is going to meet this particular promise.
I continue quoting:
To assure the objectivity which Indians of Canada have the right to expect after years of procrastination-
That is sort of an admission of self guilt by the Liberal Party.
-Commissioners may be appointed from other parts of the Commonwealth such as New Zealand, where achievements in this field are regarded as outstanding. It is Liberal Policy that the Commission will be unbiased and independent.
It is true that this was a qualified promise, since it states they "may be" appointed. None the less, when Liberal Party spokesmen took this pamphlet in their hands to explain it, this became a solemn pledge that when the Commission was established it would include people from other nations whose success in this field is supposed to have been outstanding. It goes on further to say:
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
It Is Liberal policy to establish the Indian Claims Commission on a continuing basis-
The Minister said a while ago that it is not going to be continuing at all, that it is to have a specified life.
They further promised to refer to that Commission "such contentious questions as the income tax status of Indian fishermen." I would like to know whether the Minister still believes in that promise and intends to carry it out; and will this subject matter be referred to the Commission, because the Indian people themselves will not be able to raise it under the terms of the bill. They are precluded from making a claim of that nature. I would like to ask the Government whether it remembers that solemn pledge to the Indian people, especially those in B.C. This pamphlet goes on and on, and comparing the pamphlet with the bill it is nothing but a lot of hypocrisy, a lot of deceitful promises to the native Indian people.
Yesterday the Minister made a couple of statements which are worth commenting on. As recorded at page 2686 of Hansard he stated:
-some Indians feel such a Commission would be just another device concocted by the whites to
DEBATES	2761
Indian Claims Commission whittle away Indian rights. We must do our best not only to establish this Commission as soon as possible, but when it is set up we must do what we can to ensure that everything is done to correct and remove any such impression.
Unfortunately the Minister defeated his own purposes and his own ideals by not making the necessary changes in Bill C-130. The Minister went on to say:
The Bill.. .includes several suggestions that were made by the Indian bands and others since the Bill of December, 1963 was introduced.
I do not know what the Minister means by "several" but there are only three changes of any substance in the Bill. One is that there will be a native Indian person appointed to the Commission, something which I had spoken about earlier and wondered why it was not contained in the 1963 bill. The other is that the time limit for presentation of claims is extended from two to three years, a rather insignificant change. The third is the new clause 32 which proposes the financial assistance for the presentation of claims.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister also had some interesting comments to make about the bill, and I think they require some examination. As recorded at page 2716 of yesterday's Hansard the Parliamentary Secretary said:
Indian bands or groups will be able to put forward claims-
I made note of that statement when he was speaking last night but wanted to make sure of it, and having checked Hansard I see I heard correctly. That is either misleading or it is merely reflecting the hope and desire of the Parliamentary Secretary, because there is no reference in the bill to people other than bands as groups of people who can present claims. I wish there were. In fact the definition of the word "band" is restrictive in the extreme.
The word "band" is of European extraction. It is a non-Indian word. It is a word developed by the English speaking people to apply to a particular group of Indian people, and it is alien to their thoughts. You cannot arbitrarily establish groups of people and call them bands. Bands, as such, never existed in the Indian social, political or economic structure.
If the Bill had said that bands, or nations, or tribes or other groups, or something broad of that sort, then it would open the door wider and permit the proper groups of native Indian people, by their own designation, to present claims. It is restrictive to limit it to a band. I think the Parliamentary Secretary
June 22. 1965

Indian Claims Commission was just expressing a hopeful desire rather than misleading the House and explaining something that was not the case.
The Parliamentary Secretary further said, and I think this is revealing:
This legislation means the acceptance of a legal and moral obligation by the Government of Canada to assure that Indians can have their day in court.
That to me is extremely revealing, especially when coupled with the statement of the Minister earlier today that there is some desire to see finality brought to these claims. There is a desire to end once and for all the possibility that Indians may raise claims against the Government in its dealings with them. I submit this is one of the major reasons for the presentation of this bill in almost identical form to that which was introduced in December, 1963; namely, so they can say the Indian people can have their day in court; not so their claims can be dealt with fairly and justly, but merely that they can be given the opportunity to plead their case; not so that any determination can be made on the basis of justice, but merely so the opportunity will be given for the Indian people to argue their point of view.
The Indian people of Canada have been arguing their claims against this and preceding Governments for donkeys' years, at least as far back as 1910 so far as the B.C. Indians are concerned. They have had their day in the Minister's office time and time again. They have had their day in the Indian Affairs Branch time and time again. They have argued before parliamentary committees time and time again. But nothing happened. All we have now is another agency of Government in order to provide the native Indian people with another opportunity to have their day in court. There is no desire to solve anything. There is no sincere attempt to meet their claims with fair play. There is just the desire to be able to say "We are giving you this so-called day in court." That is not good enough.
Clause 7 of the bill-and I only make reference to it in passing-is the key part of the bill, because it establishes the power of the Commission at hearings and says what the Commission may or may not do. It is true, as the Minister said, that the bill waives the normal rules of evidence so far as courts are concerned. That is an admirable course to take, but even though the Commission in hearing any claim shall not be bound by the legal rules of evidence, even though it can let native Indian people argue and present their history, which many of them only know by

story and which in many cases was never written down or documented so far as the area they owned or used was concerned; even though the Commission will let the Indian people have their day in court, as the Parliamentary Secretary said, the Commission cannot make an award on the basis of evidence which it receives and which is not covered by the legal rules of evidence. It cannot make an award unless there is evidence in writing that is reasonably contemporaneous with the time when the subject matter of the claim arose. The subject matter of some of these claims arose many decades ago. The subject matter of many of these claims predates Confederation itself by many years, as the Minister has admitted. The subject matter of these claims in many instances arose at a time when there was no written evidence, at a time when the Indian people did not keep records. The Indian people of this nation did not have title to their land in their pockets. They did not measure plots of land 60 x 120 in extent and say "Here is our land and we have pieces of paper to prove it". They held their land in common, and they held it in trust for future generations.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Where would one find written evidence which is reasonably contemporaneous with those times? Even in our archives it would be impossible to find it. As a matter of fact, from what little knowledge I have of the archives it would be virtually impossible to find anything else there, either, because there is such a chaotic mess over there.
If they cannot produce evidence in writing to support their claim there is an alternative. They can give oral evidence which is corroborated in a material particular by evidence other than oral evidence. Presumably this would be written or documentary evidence. I presume there are two kinds of evidence, that which is spoken and that which is presented in writing. Perhaps the Commission will be able to travel north of Terrace along the road to the Nass River valley and study some of the Indian petroglyphs which have been cut into the rocks back in the stone age-we do not know precisely when-by our Indian people. Possibly the Commission will be able to take cognizance of them and conclude that someone was there centuries ago.
The fact is that clause 7, as a result of the restrictions it contains, will preclude the Commission from accepting evidence presented by the Indian people unless the conditions laid down elsewhere are met, namely that it be
June 22, 1965

corroborated by written or documentary evidence. I submit this places too great a restriction on the Indian people, and forces them to submit to rules which they may not be able to observe and which stack the cards against them.
There are other provisions in this bill with which I do not agree. They make similar restrictions and will similarly prevent people from presenting their claims and receiving awards on the basis of their evidence and in accordance with fair play and justice. Regardless of the intentions of this Parliament or of the Government or of the Minister, there will be no Anal and conclusive settlement of Indian claims until the Indian people themselves feel they have been given a fair deal by this Commission. If they do not feel they are getting a square deal they will either boycott the Commission and refuse to present their claims to it, while persisting in their demand for fair play and justice, or they will appear before the Commission without any hope of receiving redress of their grievances, and still persist over the years in trying to get fair play and justice from the Government.
Only if this bill contains the basic elements of equity and justice, and only if the Indian people feel they are being fairly dealt with and can see that these principles are contained in the measure, will a final and conclusive settlement of these claims be achieved.
I for one in this Parliament would not be interested in the least in making a final determination about Indian claims unless I could be satisfied that the Indians themselves would accept it as a final and just settlement. Final settlements of Indian claims are not one sided affairs. We have had too many one sided final settlements of Indian claims. I mention only the British Columbia land question, which as far as the Government is concerned was settled finally and conclusively on five different occasions. Because it was not fair, because it was not just, and because the Indian people did not feel they had any part in the procedures which led to those decisions, there was no final settlement in their minds.
This should be our sole objective; not to make final and conclusive settlements as far as we are concerned; not to carry on the double talk of the past, but to be prepared to make a final and just settlement of Indian claims-final and just in the opinion of the Indian persons themselves. This we must do

Indian Claims Commission if, even in part we are to correct the injustices of other years.
At this stage, bearing in mind the reluctance or refusal of the Minister to declare his intention to receive or accept amendments which the committee might offer, I think we would be opposed to this bill. The hon. gentleman was asked last night by the hon. Member for Peace River whether his Government was prepared to accept amendments to the bill which might be suggested by the joint committee after the Indian people had had an opportunity to present their ideas with regard to it, in order that whatever decisions were finally made would be accepted as fair and equitable. If the Minister would make such a commitment to Parliament when he closes the debate, or at some other time should he so desire, I believe there would not be too much opposition to the passage of this bill as it now stands, although we believe we should try through some other procedure to improve the letter and spirit of certain clauses of it. If the Minister would make this commitment perhaps we could proceed on the basis of qualified acceptance. Otherwise I think we must reject it.

Mr. Speaker, if I rise to say a few words at this time it is because in my constituency of Quebec-Montmorency there is a reservation of Hurons who, I am sure, will want to make representations to the new commission, the composition of which Bill No. C-123 seeks to alter.
Furthermore, I should like to pay homage to a tribe which recently elected a new council composed of dynamic and well-intentioned young Indians who really want to help this Huron tribe to participate in the development of their community.
Moreover, I should like to warn the minister against the provisions of section 7 stating that a claim must be supported by evidence in writing or, at least, by oral evidence which would have the same value. I should also like to point to him that recently a distinguished Indian of the province, Mr. Jean-Paul Nolet, an announcer with the CBC, himself an Abenaki of the Odanac region, said, following the presentation by the National Film Board of the film entitled Le Festin des Morts, that there were so little evidence in writing that it would be very easy for those who want to abide by such evidence, relating facts which are absolutely untrue, to ignore Indian claims.
2764	COMMONS
Indian Claims Commission
As a matter of fact, he complained quite seriously that the subject matter of the film Le Festin des Marts was tendencious and based on no written documents, except for a few excerpts from "Relations" published by the Jesuit Fathers.
Consequently and following this evidence, I should like to point out to the minister that he should take for granted that tribes could submit evidence which would not necessarily be evidence in writing, in short, evidence which would not necessarily be taken from a conversation and some evidence in writing, but rather from Indian hereditary background which would really permit them to enjoy the use of a property or properties for which they were responsible many years ago, even more than a century ago.
Mr. Speaker, it should be kept in mind that in certain regions, more particularly in the Lorette reserve, located in my constituency, large tracts of land have been surrendered either by the tribe itself, or by the agent of the department or by others performing duties for both the department and the tribe.
The Lorette Indian reserve is actually confined within a territory which is much too small and which even a financial compensation would add nothing to the land of these Indians who have to live in this reserve which is too small for them. I hope the commission will take those facts into account when it is considering the request of Indian bands and even try to obtain more land for them so that they may continue community living on a reserve if they so desire.
Everybody knows that the way of life, tastes and aspirations of the Indians who live in the various parts of Canada differ from one band or tribe to the other. Consequently, compensation awarded to Indians of British Columbia, for instance, would be totally inadequate as compared compensation given to Indians of a reservation in the province of Quebec or elsewhere, more particularly to the Huron reservation of Lorette.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to provide this information to the minister so that he could give full consideration to the recommendations that will be made not only concerning financial compensation but also with respect to a new allocation of land that would allow Indians to keep their reservation and to increase their numbers.
I am pleased that the minister has announced that this legislation will be referred to a joint committee for the convenience of those who have representations to make to

the government. In addition, like the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), I hope that the minister and the government will welcome the recommendations made by the various Indian bands of the country, which, as I stated a moment ago, have different aspirations, according to the place where they live.
I am convinced that the minister will be fair as always, that he will allow the Indians who appear before the committee to make recommendations and that he will try to have those recommendations adopted to facilitate the enforcement of the regulations of the Indian claims commission.
Mr. Speaker, it must be remembered that this legislation is not meant to protect the government against the Indians but rather to enable the latter to enjoy their vested rights, their natural rights, in short to protect them against the government and the rest of the Canadian people.
I hope that the minister will dictate to the Indian Claims Commission the philosophy it must follow, making it clear that it is created to protect the Indians and give them all they are entitled to, even if some rights do not exactly correspond to the provisions of the law. In fact, the commission should take into account the general interest of the Indians and not only that of the government. I am convinced that justice can be done with regard to all Indians, wherever they live in Canada. Moreover, I am convinced that the various Indian tribes will greatly benefit from this if all the factors I have mentioned are taken into account.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to add a few words to the debate on the second reading of Bill C-123, to provide for the disposition of Indian claims. I, like many other Members of the House, am very fortunate to have an Indian band in my riding, and I have always been very interested in their welfare.
In looking over the bill I support its general provisions, with a few exceptions which have been very adequately pointed out by my colleague the hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), who preceded me. I think the bill is quite an improvement over the proposals presented to the House in the fall of 1963. At that time our party and most of the Opposition took a pretty strong stand against the proposals, regarding them as
June 22, 1965

inadequate, but I think due to the representations made by our Indian friends themselves and the advice given by the Opposition at that time, the Government has now incorporated in this bill a lot of good, sound propositions.
In general, the main reasons why it is considered necessary to establish an Indian Claims Commission under special legislation I think I can enumerate briefly. There is a legacy of bad faith in the minds of the Indians which still has to be overcome. Some of their claims are not unreasonable but it is difficult to deal with them in the courts because of technicalities. It is desired to bring an end to some of these claims which have persisted for years and years. It is hoped to deal with all past claims by establishing a cut-off date by which claims must be filed. These principles have been incorporated in this bill.
There are a variety of claims which can be made, and I should like to enumerate one or two of them for the enlightenment of the House. The establishment of an Indian Claims Commission has been advocated for many years by Indians and by others to right the wrongs which the Indians claim they have suffered in their dealings with the white man, dating back to the early days of settlement. The claims range all the way from taking land without proper compensation being agreed upon by treaty or otherwise, the failure to discharge fully treaty obligations, and improper use of Indian trust funds, to general claims based not in law but on an alleged failure by Canada to deal honourably, fairly and in good conscience with the Indians.
The advantages of this new legislation over the 1963 bill are summarized roughly as follows. The term for consideration of the claims has been extended from two years to three years. The Indians will be given legal assistance in establishing their claims, which I think is a very important improvement over the original proposals of 1963. They will be given financial assistance in establishing their claims. This, of course, is also of great importance because of the financial incapacity of our Indian friends in many cases. The clause dealing with the Indian claims court is also a very important step.
I also note that in setting out the duties of the Commission staff other employment is prohibited. I think that is an excellent thing. It is good to know that this Commission will dedicate itself to working directly, intimately

Indian Claims Commission and consistently with the problems of the Indians alone. In other words, it will not be dividing its attention between this and other matters, so that the Indians will really feel that we are taking a serious look at the situation.
I do not want to take up the time of this House because I think we have already had a very good discussion. I was a little disturbed by the carping attitude of some of our friends in the N.D.P. about this legislation, because by and large it seems to me to be worthy of support. I feel that the Government is taking a proper stand in placing this resolution before the House and I look forward to its being considered by a joint committee at an early date. I am sure it will expeditiously be transferred into legislative action for the benefit of our first Canadians.
