Mr. Speaker, I do not recall during the time I have been a Member of this House ever experiencing such a strange mixture of feelings as that which came upon me last night after examining the terms of the bill now before us. My feelings were of sorrow, rage, shame and disappointment. It seems to me quite incomprehensible that a Government of Canada, after having laboured for so long and so mightily in respect of the presentation they intended to make to us, should have produced the mouse they have produced.
The hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) made reference to the fact that the bill we are now discussing is almost identical in its important particulars to the one introduced last December, although he did point out certain minor changes that have been proposed.
When the Minister spoke on second reading, he indicated that he had received some 300 letters and briefs containing suggestions of changes to the draft bill that was circulated particularly among the Indian people across Canada. I was reasonably optimistic when I spoke yesterday at the resolution stage that when we had an opportunity of reading the bill we would find that we could accept it and give it our support with reasonably happy hearts. I am saddened and angered because, as far as I am concerned, that is not the case.
I find it difficult to comprehend how in this day and age, in the kind of world in which we as descendents of Europeans live- and I made some reference to this yesterday -it is possible that such an utter lack of imagination could be exercised in this kind
June 22, 1965

Indian Claims Commission whom I have had the opportunity to get to know best. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that I am convinced in my own mind that the Indian people are now ready and willing under some proper arrangement to let bygones be bygones, but it they are going to feel that bygones are bygones the method of bringing this about has to be based on a much broader concept and a much broader framework than this bill provides. They have to feel that they have been treated as are the people of Africa and Asia who are being given their freedom. It seems to me that the kind of concept that our Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) was talking about in London in respect of Rhodesia is the kind of concept that should be put into this bill. If it comes to that, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be more fitting if the Prime Minister of Canada were in this House concerning himself with promulgating this concept here as it relates to our own aborigines than in London concerning himself with the people of Rhodesia.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I should like to propose an amendment to the motion for second reading. I move, seconded by the hon. Member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch):
That Bill C-123 be not now read a second time, but that in the opinion of this House consideration should be given to the introduction of legislation that will provide for
(a)	an Indian Claims Commission enabled by its terms of reference and its composition to assist the Indian peoples of Canada to prepare for disposition of all outstanding claims arising out of the occupation by non-Indians of territories now within Canada; to search out and hear evidence in relation thereto and to make such awards, both general and particular, as are just and fair, and
(b)	an Indian Claims Appeal Court, the Presiding Officer of which shall be a jurist, other than a Canadian citizen, of international repute, which shall hear appeals from any decision of the Commission.

It appears that the explanatory note indicates the intentions of the company, but I think the mover should have explained them. It was explained to me that there is an interest to keep the price range of the stock within the reach of those who purchase stock on the market, namely around $20 to $25. The reason for this, as explained to me by the company, is to allow more people to participate in the stockholding of the company. It would also bring the price within the range of Canadians, thus making it easier for more Canadians to participate in the company.
If this explanation is true, and I believe it is, when the bill returns from committee I would be prepared to move a motion to split the stock still further, because I should like to see an additional split. It is worthy of note that it has already been split ten for one, and it is now being split five for one, which in effect means that the original issue has multiplied 50 times. If the argument that bringing the stock within a reasonable range would allow more Canadians to participate in the stockholding of the company does hold water, at the present market value, which is about $88 a share, the present split would bring the price to about $18. But splitting the stock again ten for one would have the advantage of bringing the stock value down to approximately $1.80 to $2 per share, with the result that this would accomplish the end explained by the company and would be in keeping with the suggestions which have been made, that the lower the price of the stock

the more opportunity would be provided Canadians to buy the stock of this company.
About 25 per cent of the total capital of this company is in stock, the remainder being in bonds at very low interest rates. This makes it possible for the company to pay a better than average dividend, better than that which they have regularly been paying for a number of years. I would suggest this explanation is much more honest than the one advanced last year, which was that if we reduced the stock value it would allow workers in the company to buy it. That was a lot of eyewash, as I think everyone who looked at the bill was aware. The company was not issuing half a share of stock every pay day, or anything like that, but was issuing certain stock over periods worked by the employees of the company. It seemed unreasonable to me that an employee would receive one share for $9 or even ten shares for $90, and that this would apply on a monthly or pay day basis. Therefore an agency would buy shares on behalf of the employees, so it really did not make any difference in relation to the cost of the stock. [DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
The argument being used is one which would probably be accepted by most companies in this field who feel that when a share reaches a value of $100 it is in a class the average purchaser cannot afford. This means that for 90 shares a purchaser would have to pay $9,000. This is not considered to be a large block in the investment picture. The smaller blocks are difficult to come by, and therefore are not in keeping with opportunities flowing to individual purchasers with a desire to purchase stock of the $10 to $20 class.
I see nothing wrong with the explanation made and I hope the committee will be able to ascertain the advantages of stock splitting in terms of greater participation by individuals wishing to purchase small amounts. I hope some consideration will be given to more extensive stock splitting so that these companies will not have to return to parliament every two or three years, as they have done in the past, to split the stock five to one, but will be allowed to split them 50 to one.
In order to give an opportunity to other Members to participate in the debate on this matter, I am prepared to allow this to be referred to the committee in the hope that it will give some consideration to the discussions which took place last year. The com-
June 22, 1965

mittee of this year should take advantage of the suggestions and discussions of last year's committee so that these companies will not have to return to parliament in a short period of time for a new stock split.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal very briefly with this bill because recently the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) made a very interesting decision resulting in the inclusion in a bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act of a bill which I have introduced in the house for the third time.
When I introduced my bill, I said that in fact our bank notes bear a deceiving reference, which could mislead the public with regard to its true nature. In fact, on our bank notes it is said that they are payable to bearer on demand.
Every member in this house knows that since 1940 our bank notes are not backed by a gold reserve. That is why I introduced this bill; it is useless for our bank notes to bear this reference which is misleading for the public.
I remember very well hearing some people use this as an argument to prove that our currency is still backed by gold. As a matter of fact, that guarantee was removed in 1940, and the Minister of Finance himself stated recently as recorded in Hansard, on page 1282:
A related amendment is proposed in respect of notes of the Bank of Canada to remove the description "payable to bearer on demand". Since these notes are themselves legal tender and have never, in fact, been convertible into gold, the present wording is unnecessary and in some quarters liable to misinterpretation.
Therefore, I was very happy when the Minister of Finance made that statement, because it confirmed the principle of the bill I introduced in the house for the third time. It was on that occasion that I expressed publicly my satisfaction and said that the minister had actually incorporated my bill in his.
In view of the circumstances, I do not think a lengthy discussion of the subject is necessary at this time. In fact, my bill is being incorporated in the minister's bill and will be passed when the government's legislation itself is enacted by the House of Commons.
Anyhow, I avail myself of this opportunity to thank the Minister of Finance for having

kindly incorporated this bill in his, thus proving that my proposals in that respect were sound and factual, in spite of newspaper reports that may have been published from time to time and which seemingly endeavoured to show to the public that the matter was of no great importance. Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-9 introduced by the hon. Member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Cote) is in my humble opinion a very excellent bill. The explanatory note is quite interesting. It reads as follows:
The purpose of this bill as stated therein is to provide that bank notes shall not be inaccurate and misleading. These notes being legal tender, it is misleading for such words to be printed on Bank of Canada notes.
I cannot quite agree with the hon. Member's explanatory note in all respects, but in some respects I do. I cannot agree with him when he takes objection to the words "will pay to the bearer on demand" because I would think it is much better to have bills payable to the bearer on demand than to have bills that are payable on a due date possibly five years from now. I do not think a one dollar bill or any other bill would be of very much use to the public, financiers or financial institutions if it were not payable to the bearer on demand.
To go back to the origin of money, it seems to me that the original bills that were circulated really evolved from the promissory notes that people used and bills had to be payable to the bearer on demand to be of any utility in trade and commerce and banking circles.

There are a few reasons why I am opposed to this bill. I am not raising a point of order at this time but it would seem to me that if this amendment were made it would be necessary to withdraw our currency. It would have to be re-issued, and the process would be expensive.
If we are to do this at all, we must be perfectly sure of the reasons for doing it. I think the proof of the pudding is that the present system works. You can take these notes into a store and buy anything you like as long as you have enough of them. I suggest that if we make a change of the kind now proposed, we should do a complete job; we should not make one specific change without bringing in a great many other changes which might result in improvements. I will give a brief indication what some of these things might be.
At present, for instance, our bills come in a series of colours. We might improve them by changing the colour system. Lumi-

nous paint of various colours might end the business of groping in the dark to find the particular unit of currency we are looking for. In the second place we might improve the over-all artistic character of our bills. I happen to have a ten-franc note in my pocket; I have been carrying it around for some time. As a piece of art work it is infinitely superior to our own bills. If we are altering our currency or changing the design we ought surely to try to make it more attractive.
Then we might give serious consideration to changing the denominations. Who can go into a store today and buy anything costing $1 or $2 or $5 or $10? I think we should introduce new denominations of $1.98, $3.98, $4.99, and so on. This would be useful and it would avoid having our pockets full of coppers, which we only lose, anyhow.
There is another suggestion which the House might consider at the same time. Perhaps we could leave blank spaces on parts of the new bills. All of us have had the experience of being in a telephone booth at some time or another. We get a message we need urgently to take down; we scramble for a piece of paper on which to write it. We find nothing. But most people generally have a dollar bill in their pockets. If there were a little blank space left on it, it could serve a dual purpose-not only spending money but a space on which to jot down notes until they can be transferred to a more permanent place.
The hon. Member may have valid reasons to advance in favour of the change he wants to bring about. I think I have valid reasons for mine. So let us hold up passage of this bill until we can bring about a real overhaul of our paper currency.

I do not propose to detain the House long on this question of Indian claims. I was struck by the comment of one of the Members of the Official Opposition who expressed surprise at the attacks made on this measure by Members of this party. I would point out that it is no coincidence that those from this party who have attacked this legislation all come from British Columbia. There is a reason for this. We in British Columbia are closer in time to the degrading experiences to which the native population has been subjected. Those of us who have friends among the Indian population know from personal contact with them the sort of treatment they and their fathers have suffered. It is so recent, in British Columbia; memory need go back no further than this.
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
I am disturbed by the fact that this bill makes no effort whatsoever to deal with what I would call the intangible injuries inflicted on these people-the deep psychological wounds which cannot be measured in the narrow, legalistic terms of the bill before us, now. I have a great many Indian friends. A few years ago when I was in Vancouver I received a message from one of the Indian chiefs off the coast of British Columbia. He was an extremely eminent Indian leader, a man who, I have not the slightest doubt, if fate had placed him in different surroundings, would have been, not chief of the Cape Mudge tribe of the Kwatkiutl Indians, but Prime Minister of this country. He was a man of tremendous capacity, intelligence, shrewdness and perception who, on becoming chief at the age of 18, saw what

Indian Claims Commission would happen to his people with the beginnings of the white invasion of his country and forcibly wrenched them out of their primitive surroundings and made them equip themselves to cope with the white man's world.
A few years ago when living in Vancouver I had a message from this old gentleman to ask me if I would take two of his grandsons into my household in Vancouver so that they could go to high school there, because the local high school close to where he lived refused to take Indian children. We took the two boys into our household and one could not find two nicer young men anywhere. Yet this is what they had been subjected to. Those lads knew that they had been sent down there because their white neighbours on that part of Vancouver Island decided that they were not good enough to attend school with their children. Then there have been other specific cases where other intangible injury has been done to them.
I was interested to hear the Minister speak earlier in rather contemptuous terms of all the other "ologies" suggested as the sort of disciplines and vocations members of the Commission should perhaps have been trained in. I would suggest to him that that expression Which he used this afternoon indicates that he knows very little, very little indeed, about what has been done to the Indian population of the province which he represents as a Member of the Cabinet. I did not use contemptuous language this afternoon. I referred to the fact that suggestions had been made regarding the use of anthropologists, sociologists and I said a number of other "ologists" had been included. I was not being contemptuous; I was using it as a descriptive phrase, and the hon. Member is now repeating his earlier remark. 1 ask that he withdraw it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Then if I misunderstood the Minister, I will willingly withdraw; but on the other hand it seemed to me that I distinctly heard a somewhat contemptuous inflection in his voice when he said "and I do not know how many other ologies had been suggested". To me this bore the connotation of a certain contempt for the suggestions. However, as the Minister has said he had no such intention, I am ready to apologize to him for having not put words into his mouth but perhaps put inflections into his voice.
Let me come to a more concrete case of injury to the Indian people, inflicted this time by the Indian affairs officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare. Among my Indian friends there is a young man who went to school with my children, who is a close personal friend of my son's, a young man who is now a chief in his tribe. He is also a teacher and he was teaching at the time at the school in Hazelton, which is an amalgamated school; that is to say, he described it to me as being attended by approximately 50 per cent white children and approximately 50 per cent Indian children.
In 1960 this young man came to visit me in my home on Vancouver Island. He happened to be down visiting his family and he called on us as old friends. He told me of a horrifying experience he had had at Hazelton when he and his fellow teachers were instructed by officials of the Federal Government
June 22, 1965	COMMONS
in the Department of National Health and Welfare that the Indian children were to attend in rotation a dental clinic which had been set up for three days in Hazelton to deal with Indian dental problems.
They despatched the children as instructed, so many at a time, and he said that it was not until well through the first day that they suddenly realized what was happening to these children. When the children came back to school their mouths were streaming with blood. The staff, including my young Indian friend, made inquiries and found that these dentists who had been sent by the Government of Canada to deal with the dental problems of the native population were not even contemplating saving teeth; they were extracting them, and it seems to me extracting them, in view of the condition that Gordon Reid described to me, in a very clumsy and inefficient way.
My colleague the hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), who then, as now, was a Member of the House-I was not then a Member of the House-asked questions of the then Minister of National Health and Welfare and eventually got the figures regarding these extractions. On the three days on which these teeth were extracted at Hazelton 103 permanent teeth were extracted from those Indian children. I cite this as an example of the sort of treatment our Indian people have had. Many of their wrongs, I would say their most damaging and brutal wrongs, have been of an intangible nature, of the nature that strips human beings of dignity and self-respect because they are looked down on with contempt.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we will not be able to deal with this question, which is the real question, on the basis of strict legality with regard to claims of land and property of various sorts. There is something much more fundamental involved. I should like to see this Commission empowered to take evidence from those who are trained in sociology, anthropology and history, who could tell the Commission of the effects of the white occupation of Canada on the native population, so that the Canadian people-those of us of nonIndian origin-would be aroused and alerted to the appalling crimes which have been committed in our name. I do not see how we can do this if we are not going to allow anybody to appear before that Commission who has not in his hands documentary proof of some material damage inflicted on some Indian or band of Indians. We are not going to be able
DEBATES	2779
Indian Claims Commission to arouse the Canadian population to the responsibilities on their shoulders to do something at this time for these people.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
I mentioned earlier that there was evidence to support those of us in British Columbia raising the loudest and sharpest protest about this resolution. In British Columbia the native Indians have not yet been driven to the conditions of those I have seen who lived in other provinces, who are now a pitiful remnant, without hope of rehabilitation, with everything gone. In spite of the treatment they have received in British Columbia and the diseases they have acquired from white conquerors of the country, they have by fighting made a comeback. I am proud to say that in my own constituency two Indians very carefully and skilfully forced a case in respect of some of their rights in British Columbia, as I am sure the Minister is well aware. They deliberately broke the game laws of British Columbia and successfully appealed to the higher courts a conviction of a magistrate. I understand there is a possibility that the Province of British Columbia will further appeal this case to the Supreme Court of Canada.
This action was taken by these people to underline the high handed manner in which all their claims to land and property in British Columbia have been swept to one side without, as my colleague for Skeena (Mr. Howard) this afternoon suggested, even a semblance of legality.
I was disturbed to find in the bill that, while there is provision for action against the Crown in the right of the province before Confederation, there is no provision whatsoever to deal with different agreements and undertakings signed by representatives of the Hudson's Bay Company on Vancouver Island, in respect of various Indian tribes, relating to land on that Island. I do not know whether the Minister is aware of this, but there are in existence three copies of a series of undertakings and agreements drafted and signed by James Douglas who, at that time, was the chief factor of the Hudson's Bay Company and who later became the Governor of the Crown Colony of Vancouver Island. These copies, in concise detail, set out the area that the Hudson's Bay Company undertook to leave in Indian hands, and set out in detail the portions of the land that the Indian population was prepared to relinquish to the Hudson's Bay Company.
2780	COMMONS
Indian Claims Commission
Since that time these agreements have simply been ignored. I suspect that a lot of people do not even know of their existence.
I happen to know of their existence because one of the copies is in the possession of a family living in my constituency, the members of which are descendants of the Hudson's Bay factor at that time. One copy has been preserved and is now in the Archives at Victoria. The third copy is in the possession of another family.
These copies set out quite plainly the agreements made at that time, and indicate quite clearly that the agreements of the day have not been broken, but swept aside. One of these agreements related to Salt Spring Island, which is an island in my constituency inhabited by some 3,000 people, as well as part of the Cowichan River Valley, an adjoining area of Vancouver Island, now thickly settled and populated. This agreement has been swept aside and the Indians in this area are confined to three small reserves, most of which comprise land of little productive value.
My fear is that if we are going to go through this matter in a legalistic way then the Commission will be faced with conclusive evidence that in this area, for instance, which is now extremely valuable property, the land was stolen from the Indians, that they have some legal claim to it, and that resulting astronomical compensatory sums will have to be paid. I am afraid the tendency will be to dismiss these claims altogether, rather than to reach an agreement which might be construed as an admission of the whole claim.
If the Government is determined to go ahead with this legislation, I hope it will also be prepared to do what the Government of the State of New York did regarding the Seneca Indians of that area, when they faced the same problem. There was a large Indian reserve in that area which was required for a reservoir for the supply of water to the City of New York. Had they been compensated for that land at its fair market value at the time an astronomical figure would have been involved. Special legislation was introduced after consultation and discussion with the Indians, and subsequently compensation was paid in recognition of their claims, to the extent of only a small portion of what they might have pressed for, had they decided to fight it through the courts.
My colleague, the hon. Member for Skeena, or the hon. Member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) pointed out this afternoon that the Indians in my part of the country are not asking for anything absurd. They know quite

DEBATES	June 22, 1965
well that although they could make out a very good legal claim to a very large part of Vancouver Island, to start with, such a claim would be preposterous and ridiculous in view of the white man's attitude. They know that such a claim would never be met. They are reasonable, adult Canadian citizens who understand enough of the white man's world to know what is possible and what is not possible. This is all the more reason why they should be treated with generosity far beyond the narrow limits set out in the bill now before us. If that is not the case I am sure the Minister will be confronted with irrefutable evidence as to enormous compensation in respect of lands which the Indian population of British Columbia does not expect to receive.
If we have a Commission that can examine these specific claims in conjunction with a scientific presentation of the appalling social effects of the white oppression of Indian people, I think we might arrive at awards to Indian people that are not measurable in material terms, but rather would be in terms of recognition of our responsibilities to these people, enabling the authorities and the Indians themselves to move forward in the development of these natives, enabling them to take their place in our society.
Sometimes there is a regrettable tendency to imagine paternalistically that all Indians are permanent children and that nothing can be done with them. No one who knows the Indians in my part of the country can subscribe to that idea.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
Very often before I come to Ottawa I am summoned by the Council of the Cowichan Indian band to attend a council meeting and to hear from them what they require me to do in Ottawa. I am always very glad to attend and I am always impressed by the ability and the competence of these people in handling the white man's world and their place in it. The last time I was on the coast I was particularly pleased to find that the eminent Indian artist, George Clutesi, of the west coast of Vancouver Island had decided to adopt my party as his political party. We were all extremely proud that a man of his eminence should have chosen our party as the one to belong to.
I am just stating these things to show that in dealing with the Indians at least in my part of the world you are not dealing with primitive savages but you are dealing with people who have suffered severe damage at our hands, people who before our ancestors
June 22, 1965	COMMONS
came to do this damage to them had developed a high culture of their own in the artistic field far ahead of anything produced by white Canada at that time. There is not, I suppose, a people on the face of the earth in whom you will find a greater incidence of oratorical ability than among the Indians of the Coast of British Columbia. In their own language and in English they are capable of speeches that I wish we could hear some times in the House of Commons for their clarity and purity of language, for sensitive choice of words and for effective presentation. Such people, Mr. Speaker, are not primitive savages; they are people who have a tremendous contribution to make to the Canadian culture.
That being so, I think it is the duty of the Government, when it is now very tardily dealing with the position of our native population, to make sure that they are enlisting the support and the aid of all the people of Canada in righting this wrong as far as we can do so; and to have that we must not be tied down to narrow, niggling, legalistic compensation for this bit of theft here and that bit of theft there. How do you estimate the compensation that is due for decades, and in some parts of the country centuries, of deep injury to the whole psychology of native people? How do you measure that in dollars? It cannot be measured in dollars. We can perhaps measure our contrition and our remorse in dollars and try now to undo some of the things that we did. As my colleague, the hon. Member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), said this afternoon, perhaps we should be looking at our native Indians more sharply than some of our people are looking at the depressed peoples in other parts of the world. So long as these people are with us we have work to do at home.
I would hope the Minister would consider what we have said from this corner of the House and widen the scope of reference of the Indian Claims Commission to include, not just material claims, but the moral claims that he and I and all the rest of us here really have to admit and really must meet. So I say again that I am sorry if I offended the Minister by putting inflections and words in his mouth. I hope I have been able to appeal to his heart, which I know is very large. I hope I have also been able to appeal to his intelligence, which I know is very high, and perhaps make him realize that he has not merely a responsibility here but a tremendous opportunity to do something that will bring lustre to the name of Canada that
DEBATES	2781
Joint Committee on Indian Affairs no other action could, by demonstrating that we are a people who for once decided that we were going to do something toward the equality of humanity within our own borders. Nothing less than that should be the goal of this legislation. Otherwise these Indian cases will not be disposed of as the legislation suggests. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I am not sure it is right to speak of being able to dispose of injuries. You can perhaps compensate to some degree for injuries, but you will not dispose of them, because after the Indians may have forgotten the injuries we did them, any of us who have any sensitivity at all are bound to remember them.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make one or two brief comments. Yesterday the hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) very ably suggested that the committee might have authority to adjourn from place to place or meet from place to place or, in other words, have the authority to travel, the idea being that by the committee travelling the native Indian people all across the country would be afforded a better opportunity of access to the committee to present their views.
As was pointed out by the hon. Member for Peace River and as anyone who was a member of the Joint Senate and House of Commons Committee on Indian Affairs in 1959, 1960 and 1961 knows very well, the committee experienced difficulty in trying to schedule particular dates for meetings with particular bands or other groups of Indian people. Members of that committee also know from experience the difficulty that the Indian people had in arranging their affairs in order to travel to Ottawa from wherever their home was to present their views and ideas and then travel back home again.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
When the Joint Senate and House of Commons Committee on Indian Affairs met a few years ago there were certain costs involved- I do not know what they were-in paying the transportation cost of the native people from their home to Ottawa, their living expenses while they were here, and their transportation cost back home. It was suggested by the hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) that we would not expend any greater amount of money if the Committee had the authority to travel. This would afford the native people in different parts of the country a better opportunity to appear before the Committee because they would have to spend less time away from their work, their family and their own activities. I do not see this authority in the provisions relating to the committee.
I should like to make a sort of last ditch appeal to the Minister to ascertain whether or not this suggestion might be given favourable consideration, with the primary concern 
being to make available to the native Indian people, in so far as we can, a full opportunity to appear before the committee and insure that no matter what we do with the bill the native people have every opportunity to present their views.

speechtext: I am sorry, but earlier today I certainly should have informed the House that, pursuant to the assurance I gave the hon. We do not consider it is necessary, in this case, to give the committee the right to travel in the way suggested by the hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). I want to assure the House, however, that, subject to what the committee itself may decide, there is certainly no intention on the part of the Government to rush the committee into bringing in an early report. The committee will have as much time as it considers necessary. The setting up of this joint committee is merely a sincere attempt on the part of the Government to make sure that the bill is in a form that will accomplish the objectives we have in mind. I can assure you that constructive suggestions that may come either from Members of the Committee or from outside will be most carefully considered by the Government.

That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act to provide for an increase from twenty-five dollars to thirty-four dollars in the amount of the monthly allowance that may be paid to a student, and to provide that, whenever the annual rate of pension payable to an orphan child under the Pension Act is changed, there will be a corresponding change in the additional amount that may be paid to a student after he has attained the age of twenty-one years.

maintopic: CHILDREN OF WAR DEAD (EDUCATION ASSISTANCE) ACT AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE MONTHLY ALLOWANCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not think it is necessary for me to go into any lengthy explanation. The resolution speaks for itself and in effect covers the bill. This is intended to bring the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act into line with the adjustments in pensions passed by Parliament earlier this year and to provide that in future, whenever there is an adjustment in the Pension Act, there will be an automatic adjustment to bring this Act into line with it.

maintopic: CHILDREN OF WAR DEAD (EDUCATION ASSISTANCE) ACT AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE MONTHLY ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure we all welcome the announcement of the Minister and the short statement he has made on this worth-while change in the terms of the Act. However, I am sure that justice and mercy strongly indicate that more generous treatment should be given.

Children of War Dead Act
I am certain that those who have served this country in war, as well as those who did not, would wish that our veterans might have their pensions kept abreast of the times by increases which, in this period of rising costs, would enable them to maintain a decent standard of living. They have earned it; we should see that they get it.
But what does the Minister give us? In this resolution dealing with the Children of War Dead, and in the following one increasing the interest paid on moneys in the Army Benevolent Fund, we have sops to the real need, a swallow when a long drink is needed. Of course there is nothing wrong with increasing the amounts to be paid for the education of each child of the war dead. The economic conditions existing today make it imperative that there should be more money for these children. Consequently we heartily approve of this measure. We wholeheartedly approve of an increase of $9 over the present $25, which is an increase of 36 per cent.
If this percentage is conceded as necessary so that the children of the war dead may be properly treated, why was there a small 10 per cent increase for the general pension of veterans last November? Where is the general increase that should be made? Is the Minister satisfied with the 10 per cent increase he announced on November 10, 1964? If he is, he is the only one who is.
The veterans organizations have made it very clear in their submissions to the Government that they are not pleased. Members of the House are not pleased either. Does not the Minister know that the earnings index in this country is rising rapidly and that pensioners are falling further and further behind the wage earnings of those they matched 45 years ago? If he does not know, then he is too ignorant to be a Minister. If he does know and does nothing, he lacks the sensibilities required for this job.
At that time it was conceded that the pensioner should have a rate equivalent to that of certain civil servants. These same civil servants today are being paid $3,500 while the basic pension rate is only $2,400. I know the Minister argues that the 100 per cent pensioner who is married with two children is the basis on which comparison should be made. However, even if this is done the pension rate has lost its former equality with wages for unskilled labour.
It is difficult to feel that the 10 per cent increase was adequate even when a pensioner, who is at the 100 per cent pension level and has children, draws the whole increase. It
June 22, 1965

Children of War Dead Act was certainly very inadequate for the 60 per cent of the war veterans who are in the 20 per cent or less disabled bracket and only receive an increase of $3.60 a month. Some 500 veterans only get 90 cents per month through the increase.
The Minister now grants a 36 per cent increase for children. To my mind by doing this he admits that 36 per cent should be a proper increase for basic pensions. Surely he does not feel that the pensioner is to be compensated in a two-fold way, once for having served his country and suffered in that service and, second, by raising children as a second obligation to his country. Everyone is not so fortunate as to have children, and those who do not should not in effect be penalized for lack of children. Many may have hesitated to have children because they realized that their disabilities condemned them to a low standard of living. Perhaps many feared that their children had too high a prospect of being fatherless in early childhood.
This great 10 per cent pension increase was the lowest ever allotted to war victims. In the four previous increases since 1920 there was a 33J per cent rise in 1951 and a 20 per cent rise in 1961. Since the wage index has been rising faster in this last period than ever before, it is apparent why we feel that the 10 per cent increase was niggardly and why we hope that the Government will consider another increase this year to bring war pensions more in line with the cost of living.
I wonder what kind of advice the Minister has had from the committee of Ministers which the Prime Minister set up to consider veterans pensions. Are they as insulated from humanitarian instincts as the Minister, and as blind to the obligations which this country owes to the men who served her in battle? It would seem so, unless the two new resolutions he mentioned today are on a different basis.

speechtext: Order. I think the point of order raised by the Minister is well taken. It might be well if we were to remain within the confines of this particular resolution.

maintopic: CHILDREN OF WAR DEAD (EDUCATION ASSISTANCE) ACT AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE MONTHLY ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since I am a Member of a group that tries so far as pos-
[Mr. Cantelon.l
sible to live within the rules, I am going to obey your instructions, even though I have a lot of sympathy for what the previous speaker said.
We in this group support the purpose of the resolution wholeheartedly because we feel the increase is necessary, owing to rising costs. This Act has been of great value to the children it was designed to serve, since it was enacted some 11 years ago. Anyone who reads the reports of the department must realize that a good number of children have received university education and other instruction as a result of this legislation.
How was this legislation placed on our statute books? It was placed there as a result of co-operation between the veterans, their organizations and the government of the day, whichever stripe it was, and with the cooperation of the officials of the department. The department in dealing with legislation hears the representations of veterans organizations before the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, considers the arguments presented in the House by Members of all parties who are particularly interested in veterans, and then co-operates with the Government in preparing legislation. In passing I may say there are 4 million people in Canada at present who are veterans or the dependants of veterans, but the point I want to make is that wherever you get co-operation of this type you find democracy functioning at its best.
The department has established precedents in several fields with respect to veterans legislation. It has dealt with hospitals, the Veterans Land Act and measures of that type. I cannot go further in this direction without being out of order.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
I do wish to stress that the veterans charter of this country, of which most Canadians are proud, was the result of co-operation between veterans organizations, the Government of the day and the officials of the department. Certain procedures have been established which might well be followed by other departments of government, as far as dealing with human beings on a successful basis is concerned.
The resolution before us is concrete in its terms. Personally, I do not see any reason for sending the bill to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. The measure is designed to do a particular job-to increase the amount of the allowance in respect of these children. Before concluding I want to say how much the veterans organizations appreciate the fact
June 22, 1965

that the Government is continuing the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. I have been a Member of this Committee for 20 years and I must say it has approached the problems of the times in a non-partisan spirit. All its Members, generally speaking, have tried to do their best, regardless of party, for the veterans and their dependants they were seeking to serve.

maintopic: CHILDREN OF WAR DEAD (EDUCATION ASSISTANCE) ACT AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE MONTHLY ALLOWANCES
speechtext: I wish only to say on behalf of our party that we agree with the purpose of the resolution before us and that we intend to support both the resolution and the bill which follows.

maintopic: CHILDREN OF WAR DEAD (EDUCATION ASSISTANCE) ACT AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE MONTHLY ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
I have one or two questions to put to the Minister. Perhaps he can give us an estimate of the number of children now covered by this legislation, together with a forecast for the future on the assumption, of course, that there will be no war in which Canadian servicemen will be killed.
I am assuming this measure covers the children of Canadians who served in the first and second world wars. There would not be any children of World War I combatants involved. There would be, from the Korean conflict.
Can the hon. gentleman tell us whether this legislation is applicable to children of Canadian servicemen who take part in peace keeping activities? Is there any elasticity in the terms of the Act? The title says in general terms: "Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act". Well, the campaign in the Congo was not a war. There are other areas in which Canadian servicemen are involved and I am wondering how strict an interpretation of this Act would be.
The Minister and I have discussed the position under the legislation covering those who served in both the first and the second world wars, of others, who were not involved in any actual war, have found themselves without coverage in terms of our veterans legislation. What steps are now being taken to include the particular category to which I have referred, bearing in mind that they are entitled to equal consideration? The case of a man killed in a training accident during the second world war is not different from that of a man killed in a similar accident on a peace keeping mission, as far as his service to the country and the needs of his family are concerned.

speechtext:

Army Benevolent Fund Act folio. His first question concerned the number of cases dealt with. These cases built up to a peak in 1961-62 when there was a total of 448 cases. I would be glad to send a copy of this list to the hon. Member. In 1962-63 there were 374; in 1963-64 there were 354. The hon. Member's second question is more difficult to answer. I would have to check the application of the insurance principle as it applies to the Cyprus operation, for instance, and the Congo. If the hon. Member would allow me, I would try to give him a more specific answer to this question when we come to second reading. Later, perhaps, I will be glad to discuss in more general terms the application to this question of principle which he and I discussed on an earlier occasion. I can only say that at the moment no final conclusion has been reached.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-118, to amend the Income Tax Act and the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
What date will the election be,
Sir?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On October 31, 1968. I indicated on the orders of the day that I would say something about clause 4 of the bill, and with the permission of the House I would like to do so now. The proposals relating to periodicals and newspapers have been criticized on a number of counts. I shall not attempt to deal with all the criticisms, some of which tend to cancel each other out, but I should like to say something about the main objections that have been expressed.
Let me begin with the periodicals. Here the main criticism, one that some hon. Members feel very keenly about, is that Time and Reader's Digest are here given resident status. Those who oppose this look upon it as a surrender to the power and influence of Mr. Henry Luce. I expect that this is the view of at least some of the hon. Members in all parts of the House.
However, other hon. Members feel equally strongly that nothing should be done to interfere with these two magazines whose Canadian editions commenced over 20 years ago. It is pointed out that both this Government and the previous Conservative Government gave clear notice in resolutions previously placed on the order paper that Time and Reader's Digest would be allowed to continue their operations in Canada. It is
June 22, 1965

argued that nothing new has happened to justify a reversal of these previous decisions.
When opinion is divided in this way there is a great temptation to defer taking action of any kind. If we were to do that, it is safe to say that the competitive position of Time and Reader's Digest in Canada would become even stronger. It is also quite probable that other foreign periodicals, including a number of trade papers, would establish themselves in Canada. If this were to happen we could kiss goodby to the chances of a Canadian magazine industry.
I do not believe there is any solution to this problem which will please everybody. However, to do nothing-to defer any action- would be the worst course of all. Accordingly the Government has accepted its responsibility and has placed a definite proposal before the House.
In doing this I would remind hon. Members of the reference in the budget speech to the subsidized postal rates now enjoyed by Time and Reader's Digest. I said that these were being studied as part of a general review of all postal rates that is now in progress, but which will not be completed until some time next fall. The legislation that will be proposed following completion of this review will eliminate the discriminatory subsidy now being given to Time and Reader's Digest.
Now let me say something about newspapers. The Government believes that control of Canadian newspapers should remain in the hands of Canadians. Parliament has provided that this must be the case with radio and television. I believe the same principle should apply to all media of communication. The Canadian Daily Newspapers Publishers Association does not take issue with this objective of the Government. However, they do oppose the method chosen to achieve it. The Government is not wedded to the particular method it has proposed for retaining control of Canadian newspapers in Canadian hands, but after 18 months of study we have not found any other method that would work satisfactorily within the powers granted the federal Government under the British North America Act. Perhaps there is another method which we have not been able to find. If so, we would be quite ready to consider it. The Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association has asked for time in which to come up with a method of achieving the objective which would be more acceptable to them. They have requested that the present proposal be deferred for a
Income Tax Act
period of months in order to give them greater opportunity to study the whole matter and, hopefully, to come up with another method that would be effective and would be acceptable to the Government.
[DOT]	(8:10 p.m.)
The Government has given most careful consideration to this request, but has concluded that it should not withdraw the present proposal pending the proposed study by the Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association. If it were to do so, some foreign interest might succeed in acquiring a Canadian newspaper before any effective method of preventing this was enacted into law. However, if the Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association finds an alternative method which would be effective and acceptable, the Government would be prepared to recommend its substitution for the present proposal at the appropriate time in the future.
Mr. Speaker, I will be only too pleased to deal with the other matters which are contained in this bill when we are in committee. I think it would probably waste the time of the House if I did so now because we would just be repeating ourselves. I think I have dealt with the matter which has attracted the most attention in recent days.

Mr. Speaker, I should perhaps first say that we trust the Minister will soon recover his health and his voice. We can see that he is suffering, and working with some difficulty. I can sympathize with a man in his position in so far as his personal health is concerned, but I do not envy his position because I think it is one of weakness. In any event, we extend to him the wish of hon. Members of this House that he recover soon.
In regard to this bill, the principle of which is to amend the Income Tax Act, there are a number of complicated provisions which we will consider in the Committee of the Whole. The bill itself is much longer and much more complicated than could be anticipated at the resolution stage. Even though it appeared complicated at that time, the resolution did not in all matters indicate the extensive amendments to certain sections of the Act that are contemplated. These are apparently the result of a seemingly simple resolution.
When we discussed these amendments at the resolution stage I made some remarks about the income tax cut of 10 per cent in respect of personal incomes, indicating that I felt this was discriminatory. Nothing has

June 22, 1965
Income Tax Act
been said since that has swayed me from that opinion. In view of the fact that the Minister has indicated that in the fiscal year 1964-65 there will be an expected growth factor of about $250 million to $275 million, it is apparent that this proposal has been politically motivated. When one assesses the comments that have been made in respect of this tax cut he can only conclude that the responsible politicians had an eye cocked toward an election, having in mind that the budget was prepared some time in March or April. Last night the Minister indicated that he would like to see an election, and I am not sure that he did not strain his voice at that time when he addressed some potential disciples in Toronto, who needed some ministerial assurance.
Perhaps I may be allowed to refer to some comments in respect of the budget which appeared in the column of Ronald Anderson, who states:
The personal tax cut, in the view of most analysts, will have relatively little impact on the economy: Canada's 10 per cent cut in personal taxes compared with a 20 per cent cut in U.S. personal income taxes.
This makes the point I was referring to the other night in regard to corporation taxes. I will develop this point a little later. The article then states:
Moreover, while the Canadian corporation tax remains at 21 per cent on the first $35,000 of income and 50 per cent on the remainder, the U.S. corporate tax has been reduced from the 1963 level of 30 per cent on the first $25,000 and 52 per cent on the remainder, to the 1965 level of 22 per cent on the first $25,000 and 48 per cent on income over that amount.
There is an expectation in the United States that the excise tax will be cut by 15 per cent by July 1, but that question has not been resolved.
One could read other editorial comments which have appeared in newspapers including the Montreal Gazette, the Toronto Globe and Mail, the Telegram and the Star, and and many others, and come to the same conclusion that the budget was based on the expectation of an election.
The Montreal Gazette of April 27 states:
The cut in personal income taxes, fulfilling forecasts, suggests either a planned election, or insurance against the possibility of an election, or a deterrent to an election by raising the government's popularity. The economy could have been stimulated as much, or more, by reducing corporation taxes. Mr. Gordon explained great changes would be premature before the report of the Royal Commission on Taxation (K. LeM. Carter) but that report will be as concerned with personal as with corporation taxes. One cut is as premature as the

other and both were regarded as premature by Mr. Gordon last year.
This year we have been told that it is premature to consider corporation income tax cuts, but this year that is not so with regard to personal income tax cuts. Both were in a premature bracket last year.
The Globe and Mail of April 27 states:
And Now What Day For The Election?...
Stimulating the economy would have required a cut in corporation tax as well. Mr. Gordon is setting the stage for a fall election. He has remembered the unions, the professional men, the farmers, uncles and aunts, even trademarks, and preserved a mass teaser for future stimulation in proposed removal of sales tax on drugs.
Then we can go west to the Edmonton Journal of April 27 which states:
These are the concessions traditionally used to sweeten up voters. If the Minister thinks he did all he could be expected to do for business, many businessmen facing keen foreign competition will not agree with him.. .Canadian finance ministers in recent years have been notoriously bad deficit guessers and Mr. Gordon is no exception. .. .The income tax cut will cushion the pension plan and there will be a time lag between incoming contributions and the borrowing and spending of the money
by the provinces____In the New Economics the
erosion of 2 or 3 per cent in the value of money is not inflationary. Be that as it may, the danger of inflation, balance of payment problems and other evils must be constantly guarded against.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, to quote from an article by Fraser Robertson which appeared in the Globe and Mail of April 28:
Budget has little to do with economic reality. It ended with a fine challenge to us all to share in Canada's great future. So how do we share? The government intends to dig $7.35 billion out of our pockets in the coming year, $214 million more than last year, and it intends to spend $431 million more than last year.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
The point is often missed that there is an increase of $431 million in expenditures.
He claims citizens can spend $170 million more than last year but what about those extra sales taxes earlier this year? And next year, when he says we shall have $265 million more in take home pay, who will be paying those extra payroll deductions for the pension plan? His tax cut is pure hocus-pocus. If it is true that the $170 million adds to purchasing power, then the extra government spending, which certainly comes out of our pockets, detracts from purchasing power by $431 million. Experience in other countries shows, and the Economic Council recommended, that capital investment does speed economic expansion, as the Canadian housing program has shown. But Mr. Gordon expects industry to hand out more jobs, better machinery for the workers, new plants and extra selling efforts with nary a penny from him.
I have spoken about the problems of the balance of payments deficit and other items which concern us from the point of view of
June 22, 1965

the maintenance of the advancing rhythm of the economy. The tax cut proposed by the Minister was designed to meet this problem. That was his stated purpose, in addition to which, of course, it would be a cushion for the payments under the Canada Pension Plan starting next January. I should like to draw to the attention of the House an article written by John Allan May who is European economic correspondent for the Christian Science Monitor. It is datelined from London under date of June 18, 1965 and reads as follows:
Now is the time when the wisdom of the world's economists is most strongly challenged-and most urgently needed. The question is: Can they tell how to halt a slide toward recession and how to restart the motors of expansion?
Too many indicators now point downward. Too few point upward. It is possibly true that only in the United States and West Germany are there any forceful signs of any expansion at all.
Even in the United States we have had men in responsible positions raise a hand of warning and make very cold and calculated speeches with regard to possible danger signs. Some people may object to this and some people may object to the tenor of my remarks tonight, but I must say that at all times we must be careful to see just what is ahead of us. It is toward the value of an income tax cut in regard to the maintenance and stimulation of the economy that I am directing my remarks.
We know that the figures for the first quarter with regard to the balance of international payments show a rather alarming increase. We also see a flattening out of the increase in our commodity export figures. If this year continues as the pace of the earlier months has indicated, we are going to finish up with a deficit on international account of rather monumental proportions, all of which is much to the concern of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It should be to the great concern of the Minister of Finance, because we know what has happened to this country in the past when there has been an overly large deficit on international account. We saw what happened in Britain last year, and at the moment they are facing the very same problem. I refer again to Mr. May's article:
In Britain the indicators now point to the introduction of direct controls over imports.
This would affect Canada.
It is thought that further controls on capital outflows also may have to be introduced. This is because the British balance of payments must be
Income Tax Act
brought back into balance, whatever way it is done. Britain cannot take on any further debts.
In so far as Canada is concerned, I suggest that we too face the problems involved in taking on an increased load of debt on international account.
The effect, however, must be to reduce world trade a little further. It seems likely that the trade of western Europe could be most severely affected...
Here is something that is very troubling.
The economic background to the Conference of Commonwealth Prime Ministers also shows storm flags flying. Every country represented, including Canada, is today in deficit on its international payments. Two of the most important in a monetary sense, Australia and India, have decided they must, like Britain, cut their spending severely. The commodity prices on which most of the Commonwealth largely depends are tending downward. Outside the Commonwealth, it is noted that Japan also is in some financial difficulties.
I trust the House will forgive me what may seem to some hon. Members to be an undue emphasis on the problems of a deficit in the balance of international payments, but to me this is a key factor with regard to the stimulation and maintenance of our economy. The Minister proposes to deal with the matter by his 10 per cent cut in income tax and there are also some capital cost allowances to industry. I put it to the Minister that the 10 per cent cut in income tax is insignificant in so far as stimulation of the economy is concerned. I think he could have done a lot better by giving an equivalent cut on the corporation tax side, or perhaps even a greater cut than he did in the personal income tax field but, of course, on the corporation side he was not dealing with votes.
My colleague from Okanagan Boundary suggests, as many analysts have also done, that something should have been done about the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and certainly on production machinery. I think this is one area where the Government will really have to re-examine its position.
In so far as much of the bill is concerned we are dealing with the closing of loopholes and there are a number of technical points involved. One has to do with the exploration for gas and oil. In order to understand the amendment a person needs to be very well versed in the corporate set-up of development and production companies with their syndicate or joint venture exploration groups, the purchase of drilling rights and reassignment back to the parent so they can be used for write-off purposes. There was a loophole as a result of an amendment made to the Income Tax Act in 1962, and as these

June 22. 1965
Income Tax Act
companies in the oil industry are astute operators in the field of corporation finance and taxation they were able to find this loophole. I am not too sure they were doing anything wrong but the Income Tax Department certainly thought it was wrong. I am not too sure that is so. I like to see as much incentive as possible given to the oil and gas industry to go out and develop the resources of the country. We can put too close a bridle on them at times.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
There is another amendment with regard to the residence rule for corporations. I think the Minister is fully aware of the implications of this change. Certainly some companies are going to be caught and there is going to be quite a scream from some corporations which have a foreign residence but which will now be deemed to be Canadian resident companies whose world income will now become subject to Canadian tax. This is the opinion of the Canadian Tax Foundation. I hope the Minister, in this particular instance, may give the House an estimate of the effect this may have, by deeming Canadian foreign resident Canadian corporations because of their operations in Canada and attracting to those companies the Canadian tax rate on their world income. I should like the Minister, perhaps, to address his attention to this particular feature and let us know just what he expects will be the effect of plugging this loophole. Perhaps he thought he was plugging a loophole and he may be doing more harm than the situation he was correcting.
We have heard the Minister's proposal with regard to periodicals and newspapers. Dealing with periodicals he says that the previous administration had the same problem. Yes, we had the same problem; but the solution was somewhat different. It was to impose a tax disallowance of 50 per cent on advertising in dealing with Time and Reader's Digest. I am not satisfied, myself, that this was necessarily the best solution. This was a proposal which had not been discussed. The Minister has had the benefit of two years' experience and re-examination of the problem. Now we are enshrining into statute law the privileges enjoyed by Time and Reader's Digest. It was against these two periodicals that the Canadian periodicals complained. They felt they could not survive in the face of the unfair competition put forward by these two periodicals. There have been changes in the past two years. There

have been changes since the O'Leary Commission reported in regard to the number of publications which have continued to exist.
Surely, however, there would have been some better solution than enshrining Time and Reader's Digest and giving them that absolute statutory protection against competition from the United States, Britain and France. This is what you are doing. You may say that Canadian periodicals are being protected from some bold, bad wolves from either the United States or abroad, but you are also protecting Time and Reader's Digest from the competition of periodicals from their own country. They have the best of all possible worlds as a result of the Government's proposals. I do not believe this is an adequate solution for our Canadian periodicals. Certainly, I do not believe the two publications that are singled out merit this rather favourable treatment they are receiving.
Now, with regard to newspapers, I need not repeat the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) or the other spokesmen from this side of the House concerning the tax on advertising in newspapers, should they become owned more than 25 per cent by foreign interests. Ever since the budget speech was delivered on April 26, we have seen a spate of editorial criticism from one end of the country to the other, from Victoria to St. John's Newfoundland. There has been the odd exception. Representatives of the Newspapers Publishers Association have seen the Minister, not once but twice. I noticed that their representative was meeting the Government last Friday. Before the Minister spoke tonight, we saw speculative news articles indicating that there might be a pause in the Government's move to impose this penalty. It is not a tax, it is a penalty.
In this regard, I have always wondered why it was deemed to affect ways and means, when there was an amendment proposed the other night. It would not affect ways and means whatever. This is merely a penalty, and something would have to be done to attract the tax. In other words, one had to transgress the rules in order to attract the tax. The Minister, therefore, could not expect, in the normal course of events, one penny of revenue. How this could affect ways and means, I fail to see. In any event, this penalty in the Income Tax Act is to be used to achieve what some people say is a laudable objective. Certainly, we would like to maintain, in so far as possible, control of Canadian newspapers in the hands of Canadians,
June 22, 1965

in the same way as we would like to maintain control of many types of operations in the hands of Canadians. I noticed one editorial comment to the effect that there was as much justification for imposing this penalty on newspapers as there would be in preventing any foreign interest from coming in and buying Clarkson, Gordon & Company and entering into the chartered accountancy field. After all, these companies have many corporate secrets. They know many things about the Canadian economy, and therefore foreign control of these companies could influence the situation in Canada. The thesis is arguable.
Well, we do not see anything of this nature in the bill. 1 do not know just what motivated the Minister in imposing this penalty to try to maintain the Canadianization of newspaper ownership. Is it that they were in particular danger? I noticed in a column written by Basil Dean, publisher of the Edmonton Journal, that there was a current rumour that certain French interests were going to try to buy into La Presse of Montreal in order to project the point of view of the French Government. Well, of course, one can build speculation upon speculation. I believe one must classify this amongst those really wild rumours, but it is still a rumour. I do not know how much it influenced the Minister or if he heard it. Were there any other newspapers that were under imminent attack by foreign owners? I am sure that foreign owners would take on Canadian newspapers or attempt to buy Canadian newspapers under the following circumstances: First, if a newspaper were in temporary difficulty and could be bought cheap, then built up into something really profitable. Frankly, the motive is economic. It is certainly not to influence thought. The second circumstance would be a successful newspaper that was a going proposition and was very attractive. It would attract a takeover bid.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
If the Minister, the Government and Canadian newspapers are so jealous of Canadian ownership there is always one solution, that they shall not sell. As a matter of fact some newspapers have voluntarily adopted measures whereby foreign takeover cannot take place. Therefore I think the Minister would have been far wiser to accede to the request of the Newspaper Publishers Association to defer this tax penalty until some more reasonable solution had been worked out to the satisfaction of the press.
Income Tax Act
Some people have suggested that the press is crying wolf, that this is an old bugaboo, that this is not really an attempt to introduce censorship. I put it to hon. Members that this is the cornerstone from which other moves could be made with regard to newspapers.
What about magazines?
I am concerned about daily newspapers.
What's the difference?

There is a great deal of difference. The hon. Member for York-Scar-borough (Mr. Moreau) can engage in a discussion of that when we reach clause by clause examination of the bill.
One can read all sorts of editorials on this subject in chain newspapers from Victoria to St. John's, in privately owned newspapers, in small, medium and metropolitan newspapers, and generally in newspapers that support the Government.
Reference was made during orders of the day today to an article in the Winnipeg Free Press of June 17, headed, "Press Control has a long History", pointing out that it started with King George III who first taxed advertising, Adolph Hitler who jailed editors, Benito Mussolini who built a subservient press, Joseph Stalin who made the press a government mouthpiece, Juan Peron who closed down newspapers, Fidel Castro who exiled editors, and winding up with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) who would tax advertising.
The other day the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) quoted from editorial comment in the same newspaper of June 16, but I will not refer to that again. The Evening Reporter in Galt has some harsh things to say about this proposal, and I think the Minister should read that editorial.
The Guelph Mercury of June 17 said:
If there is any requirement whatever to limit ownership of Canadian newspapers to Canadians, it is quite possible to effect this control without government interference and through the voluntary action of the owners. In Britain and some other European countries, the line of succession of ownership and the editorial policies of certain newspapers are effected by agreement within the proprietor companies. The governments follow a hands-off policy.
Apart from this principle, which is readily applicable within Canada, the hard fact is that the profit margin of Canadian newspapers is not so lush as to be attractive to foreign investors. They can secure larger returns on their capital with less risk, by investing in Canadian natural resource corporations.
There is, indeed, no more urgency for the prohibition fathered by Mr. Gordon than there is for

June 22, 1965
Income Tax Act
a law forbidding Americans or other outsiders from acquiring control of firms of external chartered accountants, such as Clarkson, Gordon and Company, in which the Finance Minister inherited a considerable interest and in which he was active until joining the cabinet. Accountancy firms of high repute are necessarily privy to the secrets of Canada's major corporations whom they serve, and on occasion must have access to confidential phases of government. Surely the acquisition of such firms by foreigners would raise problems of much delicacy.
The Sarnia Observer of June 18 has this to say:
The free press of Canada is threatened by legislation now making its slow progress through the House of Commons.
It isn't threatened today, or perhaps tomorrow. But some time in the future, the machinery now proposed by the Government can be used to effectively muzzle any newspaper-or all newspapers.
This is a matter of argument but I put it to the Minister and to the hon. Members that he is trying to accomplish something the Wrong way. I would have appreciated it if the Minister had not stood up in this House the other day and, in a moment of bravado, said the Government would stand or fall by this measure. Are we again under a threat? Is this some chest thumping on the part of the Minister? I do not know, but I think he in reasonableness would have agreed to the newspaper publishers' request to defer this matter, had he hot made that rather unwise and brash statement the other night. He put himself in a box and now we are told we are going to have this proposal on the statute books.
I would not say that the House is being bribed, but it is being asked, "Pass this little bit of legislation and if we find something better in the future, then we will substitute that for it." Is this a proper way to do things? If this measure is bad it should not be put on the statute books, and the Government should recognize that this is not the most satisfactory way to deal with the problem.
Is there any particular rush? What is the rush, that newspaper owners must be protected? Is the Montreal Gazette about to be taken over, or the Toronto Star, or the Vancouver Sun? Is this something that is over the horizon, or is there something in this that involves Lord Thomson? I do not know what the reaction of my hon. friend from Port Arthur is going to be when I mention that eminent gentleman's name. Is he considered by the Canadian government to be a foreigner, now that he has a title, or just what is the situation with regard to him?
Not only has this proposal been criticized in Canada but it has also been criticized in the foreign press. The Canadian Press under dateline of May 29 reports that the London Daily Mail calls it a subtle encroachment on press freedom, not very different from withholding government advertising, a favourite device for bringing newspapers to heel in countries where press revenue is scanty.
The Vancouver Province of May 21 said:
An aura of underhandedness does not sit well with many Canadians.. .dangerous to freedom of the press.. .conflicts with the interest of the public and of the newspapers themselves. I was also interested to hear the Minister of Finance suggest that the method outlined in this bill is the only way the Government could find to impose conditions which would have the objective of keeping Canadian newspapers and periodicals Canadian owned and controlled. He even went so far as to say that if anyone, be it the Publishers Association, Members of the Opposition, or anybody else, came forward with some other method of achieving this objective, the Government would be receptive to it.
I think there is a case to be made for a little more time to consider other methods of achieving this objective. The Minister of Finance suggested that to do nothing would perhaps be a disservice to Canada, because in the meantime there could be some publications purchased by foreign companies and it would be difficult to do anything about it on a retroactive basis. I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Finance to the fact that he did not hesitate when bringing in legislation respecting the ownership of banks in Canada to make a press announcement months ahead disclosing that the Gov-

ernment intended to impose restrictions on the ownership of the chartered banks of this country. Furthermore, if any province bought any shares before that legislation became fully effective, the Government was prepared to remove the voting rights from those common shares.
I think there is probably some disagreement about whether the federal Government now has the constitutional right under the British North America Act to say who shall own shares in any kind of property or company, be it banks or anything else. The Minister of Finance attempted to contend that because banking and the control of currency and coinage, and so on, comes under the umbrella of the federal Government and its statutes, it gave the Government the authority to say who could own these shares.
