maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-INQUIRY AS TO AMENDMENT OF FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canada Labour Code, even though we had to wait a long time to get it, is a good piece of legislation. It provides a minimum wage, a maximum work week, two weeks holiday with pay after one year and eight statutory holidays for all the employees who are covered by this legislation.
However, there are certain employees ostensibly in the federal field who are not covered by the code. These are in two categories- direct employees of the Federal Government and persons working on Federal Government contracts. Actually the first person to mention the fact that the Canada Labour Code would not cover these other categories of workers was the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) himself. When he moved the second reading of the Canada Labour Code on October 13, 1964, he pointed this out, as will be seen from a reading on pages 8999 and 9000 of Hansard for that date.
In doing so the Minister made clear the Government's intention later in that same session to cover these other groups of people by bringing forward amendments to the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act. The next day, October 14, 1964, in response to a question of mine as reported at page 9062 of Han-

sard, the Minister of Labour confirmed that it was the Government's intention to bring in the amendments to the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act that session, which was the second session of this Parliament, the one which ended on April 3, 1965.
While that session was still in progress, in particular on February 26, 1965, as reported at page 11770 of Hansard, I asked the Minister whether it was the Government's intention to make sure that the protection afforded by the Canada Labour Code would be extended to these other people and whether this coverage would apply by the same effective date, namely July 1, 1965. The Minister's reply was clear. He said: "That is the intention, Mr. Speaker."
A month or so later, in the present session, I asked the Minister on May 10, 1965, as reported at pages 1100 and 1101, when this would be done. His reply was: "As quickly as possible". I asked about the previous commitment with respect to July 1. On May 11 I reminded him again of this previous commitment and in reply to my questions on that date he again said the Act would be amended by July 1. This is in keeping with the commitment made throughout that these four minimum standards to which I have referred would be made applicable not only to those who come under the Canada Labour Code but to these other two groups, direct Federal Government Employees and those working on Federal Government contracts.
Time has a way of slipping by. The legislation did not appear on the order paper, so on June 3, 1965, I asked the Minister again when this legislation would be brought in, having in mind the commitment that it would be passed before July 1. The Minister's response to that question, to be found at pages 1932 and 1933, was that the parliamentary timetable was getting in the way. I asked him whether the delay was caused by representations against the legislation. His reply was that the only delay was that which had arisen because of difficulties connected with the parliamentary timetable.
On June 16, as reported at pages 2501 and 2502, I asked the hon. gentleman when this legislation was to be brought forward and again he confirmed it would be done by July 1. Yesterday, however, June 21, when I again asked the Minister about this Fair Wages and Hours of Labour legislation he fell back on the explanation that the parliamentary timetable did not permit this to be done by July 1. When I asked him what had
June 22, 1965	COMMONS
happened to the Government's promise to bring it in by July 1, his answer was that nothing had happened to the promise, that it was still the Government's intention, but that it depended on the parliamentary timetable.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
There is no argument about the substance of this matter. The Minister and I are agreed that these minimum standards should be made applicable to all the people whom the federal Government can cover. The whole question is whether or not it will be done by the date the Minister promised, namely the same date the Canada Labour Code comes into effect; and that has been established as July 1, just a week or so away.
The argument about the parliamentary timetable being the problem is now ridiculous. We are running out of Government business these days. Before we know it we shall be adjourning for a summer recess. I suggest that in view of that the Minister ought to keep his promise and bring this legislation in before the House rises for any summer recess. I say to him that if he tries to use the argument that the Prime Minister did not include it in the list of business which he announced on June 9 as the business for this part of the session, the answer is that whenever the Government comes along with something that was not in that list and somebody from the Tory front bench complains about it, some Minister in the Government gets up and says: "Read the second sentence of what the Prime Minister said"-namely that there might be emergencies. I suggest that keeping the Minister's promise is the kind of emergency which is covered in that sentence and that this legislation ought to be brought in before July 1.
There can hardly be an argument about the substance of this legislation. We fought the battle when we had debate on the Canada Labour Code. The point is to extend it to all the employees that federal law can cover. The Minister mentioned the other day that one feature only, namely the minimum wage, will apply to one part of the group, but this is not good enough in view of the fact that it is the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act itself that needs to be amended by July 1.
I would ask the Minister to do himself proud, to keep his promise, and to bring in this legislation before July 1.

There was never at any particular time-and an examination will bear this out-a commitment to have this legislation enacted by July 1, 1965. I have always talked in this context about federal employees. Employees working for contractors doing federal jobs are not federal employees by any stretch of the imagination.
We shall have covered employees in federal industries and direct employees of the Government of Canada by July 1, 1965. We will complete this three-fold effort to improve basic working conditions by making the appropriate amendments to the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act. Last session in October I expressed the hope that these amendments would be completed, but we know what kind of session it was. There were times when I did not think we would get the Canada Labour Code through or the pension plan, let alone the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour amendments. The Fair Wages and Hours of Labour amendments were forecast in the speech from the throne for this session and they will be completed at this session. I suggest to my hon. friend that if he carefully examines the Hansard record he will conclude, as I have done, that the only commitment with respect to July 1, 1965 was in connection with federal employees. At no time was there a commitment that the amendments would be completed by July 1, 1965, although I am as eager as my hon. friend to have them completed and would have had them completed last year had we had a different kind of session. However, that is now-part of history, and these amendments will be completed this session.

maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-TORONTO- PRODUCTION AND C.B.C. SHOWING OF SEX EXPLOITATION FILM
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-TORONTO- PRODUCTION AND C.B.C. SHOWING OF SEX EXPLOITATION FILM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday morning I thought it advisable to ask this question of the Department of Justice:
Will the Department of Justice be taking any action against C.B.C. employees Ted Leversuch, John Cavall, Phil Styles, Peter Douett and John Ashley, who have recently aided Independent Film Artists Limited of Toronto in producing the sex orgy film "Room for a Stranger", at Lakeshore Studios in Toronto? Is not this sex exploitation film, which features Jean Christopher, currently appearing on the C.B.C. program "Nightcap" in violation of Section 150 of the Criminal Code?
When I asked that question I was invited to place it on the order paper. No reply was vouchsafed by the Department of Justice.
This film, which is known as a "stag film" in the trade, is described in a little publication "CINE World"-I suppose the emphasis is on "CIN"-but the name is "CINE World". This booklet describes the film "Room for a Stranger" as being distributed in the United States by a chap by the name of Sam Lake, "one of the foremost distributors of sex-exploitation pictures in the world". When I saw the pictures in this little magazine, which states that it is "devoted to the art of films and filming", I immediately thought of the Criminal Code and particularly section 150 which states in part:
Everyone commits an offence who
(a) makes, prints, publishes, distributes, circulates or has in his possession for the purpose of publication, distribution or circulation any obscene written matter, picture, model, phonograph record or other thing whatsoever,-
The Code provides for a maximum sentence of two years in jail for anyone who is convicted under this section 150.
I knew there was no use asking a question in this House as to whether or not the C.B.C. had knowledge that it employed people who make these sex films after hours, because the answer would come back in 18 months, from the unsearchable depths in which the C.B.C. hides, that the C.B.C. has no knowledge of the picture in question and is, therefore, unable to give an answer. I thought, however, if it asked the Department of Justice I would get a straight, forthright answer, because that department is willing to express itself and does not shed its authority by stating it cannot answer for the actions of the R.C.M.P., or that it cannot answer for this organization or that organization. That department always gives answers; but no answer is ever forthcoming from the C.B.C.


I asked this question about this film because I could not believe it possible that the C.B.C., which produces these high quality films it is everlastingly advertising and talking about, which are much more high quality than any which can be produced by private T.V. stations, would employ such characters as produced this super picture. It is interesting to find that the characters that appear in this picture are of the very superior C.B.C. type.
After I asked the question on Friday morning, some newspapermen came around wanting to know whether I could tell them where to buy this little booklet. I told them I bought mine at the Book Cellar, located at the corner of Bay and Bloor Streets in Toronto. Someone asked: Are you accusing the C.B.C. of making this film? I said: I am not accusing the C.B.C. or anybody else of anything. I simply asked whether these people who made this sex exploitation film were going to be prosecuted under section 150 of the Criminal Code. I never mentioned the C.B.C. at all. All I did was to give the police, the Department of Justice and any other justice authorities interested in the problem, the addresses at which these people could be picked up if action should be taken. It was no concern of mine whether they were employed by the C.B.C. I just thought I might help the police officials by giving them the addresses at which these people could be found.
[DOT] (10:40 p.m.)
The C.B.C. then rushed into the act and started to give answers in reply to questions I have never asked. I am not interested in their replies. In fact, they have even gone to the point of stating that they will issue a formal statement in reply to Mr. Cowan. Since Mr. Cowan did not ask them anything he is not interested in any formal reply.
But it is interesting that when I stated that the film was made by C.B.C. employees who were moonlighting, the C.B.C. issued a statement to the Toronto Globe and Mail denying that this picture was made on moonlighting time but saying that it was made on spare time of its employees. Somebody should take the C.B.C. aside some day and ask them what the difference is between moonlighting and a spare time occupation. The rest of us do not understand, but the C.B.C. draws some kind of distinction. I am not asking the C.B.C. any questions tonight. My question is whether the Department of Justice is going to take any action against these people.
June 22, 1965

Mr. Phil Styles, a C.B.C. employee, is listed as production manager of this sex exploitation film, "Room for a Stranger". The C.B.C. might answer this question. Does he have authority to declare C.B.C. sets surplus so they can be bought by the producers of private television films at knock-down prices? If he has authority to declare sets surplus and they are bought cheaply by other people, why are they not publicly advertised for sale so that we can get the highest possible price for C.B.C. sets?
But this is not the point on which I am seeking an answer tonight. I know this film is one of sex exploitation from the description in the little paper and the pictures I have seen. Miss Christopher has told the Globe and Mail that there is a definite plot in the picture. If hon. Members could see the pictures I have seen in CINE World and could see the eyes of the actor they would know there is a definite plot all right, but Miss Christopher does not give too much detail in that regard in her newspaper comment.
I simply ask the Department of Justice: Is any action being contemplated against these C.B.C. employees who in their spare time- the C.B.C. says they are not moonlighting- are making films which are described in CINE World as sex exploitation?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. Member has brought before the House a matter of some considerable interest. Just to show the interest of all Members and others, may I say it is not very often that at this late hour we are blessed with the presence of very many members of the Press Gallery and I noticed that as the hon. Member was speaking a member of the press was standing up to look very closely at the material the hon. Member had in his hand.
I think the hon. Member probably realizes, as I am sure all other hon. Members of the House do, that the jurisdiction over these matters is divided between the federal and provincial governments. While it is this Parliament which has enacted the Criminal Code and the section with regard to obscene literature to which the hon. Member has referred, it is the function and jurisdiction of the provincial authorities and more particularly the local police authorities to take the action that may be indicated by any particular occurrence.
In direct answer to the hon. Member's question I must therefore say that the federal Department of Justice will not be taking

maintopic: EXPO '67-REQUEST FOR CONSIDERATION OF EXPENDITURES BY HOUSE COMMITTEE
EXPO '67-REQUEST FOR CONSIDERATION OF EXPENDITURES BY HOUSE COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not at all satisfied with the answer of the Acting Prime Minister with regard to the financial participation of the federal Government in Expo '67. The Canadian people were informed by the Progressive Conservative Government that they would be committed to a grant of $20 million. We are now informed that this figure has spiralled to $64 million as at the end of this fiscal year and there appears to be every indication that the federal involvement will go well beyond $100 million before it is completed.
Furthermore, there is an estimated deficit of $60 million to be faced after the fair has run its course of which the federal Government's share will be 50 per cent or $30 million. If the deficit is to balloon out of all proportion, as the estimate of the cost of building the plant has, by some 70 per cent, surely the taxpayers of this nation have the right to know that the money which has already been committed and will continue to be committed by this Government is being spent in a proper manner. I believe the Canadian people also have a right to know how many of their tax dollars will be spent on this extravaganza before another day passes. There is only one way for the Government to provide the kind of assurance the Canadian people have a right to expect in this matter, and that is through an all party committee of the House of Commons which can act as a watchdog over the expenditures and make certain the nation does not end up with the biggest unexplained white elephant in our 100 year history.
It is my understanding the C.B.C. has involved itself in a multi-million dollar expenditure without the calling of tenders to determine the best price, or the luxury of even considering alternative bids from companies other than the one they chose to do their work. Surely this cannot be allowed to continue if we are to accept our responsibilities to the taxpayers of this nation. At the same time, this Government accomplishes nothing, in my view, by trying to give the
June 22, 1965

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion impression that questions should not be asked about this financial colossus, because it is associated with our 100th anniversary and is located in the Province of Quebec. We can look forward to being too poor to attend the World Fair in 1967 if this Las Vegas spirit of the present administration is allowed to continue unchecked. A parliamentary committee is the only protection the Canadian taxpayer has to the multi-million dollar blank cheque we apparently have written.
